Git Rebase is used to move a branch to a new base commit, effectively reapplying commits on top of another branch.

🔹 Example: Rebasing a feature branch onto the main branch

# Step 1: Checkout the feature branch
git checkout feature-branch

# Step 2: Rebase onto the main branch
git rebase main

🔹 What happens? The commits from feature-branch are replayed on top of the latest main branch.

✅ When to use Git Rebase?
  • ✔️ To keep a cleaner commit history.
  • ✔️ To integrate changes from the main branch without a merge commit.
📌 3. git fetch - What is it?

Git Fetch retrieves the latest changes from a remote repository but does not merge them into the current branch.

🔹 Example: Fetching changes from remote

# Fetch changes from remote repository
git fetch origin

🔹 What happens? It downloads the latest commits, branches, and tags without modifying your working directory.

✅ When to use Git Fetch?
  • ✔️ To check for remote updates without modifying local branches.
  • ✔️ Before running git merge or git rebase.
✅ Conclusion
  • ✔️ git resolve: Manually resolving merge conflicts.
  • ✔️ git rebase: Reapply commits on top of another branch (used for a cleaner history).
  • ✔️ git fetch: Download remote changes without merging them.

A Functional Interface in Java is an interface that has only one abstract method, but it can have multiple default or static methods.

📌 Example: Creating a Functional Interface

Below is a simple example of a functional interface:


@FunctionalInterface
interface MyFunctionalInterface {
    void sayHello();  // Single Abstract Method

    // Default method
    default void greet() {
        System.out.println("Hello from default method!");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MyFunctionalInterface obj = () -> System.out.println("Hello, Functional Interface!");
        obj.sayHello();  // Lambda Expression
        obj.greet();
    }
}

✅ Output: Hello, Functional Interface! and Hello from default method!

The Runnable interface is used for defining a task that runs in a separate thread. 


public class RunnableExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("Thread is running...");
        new Thread(task).start();
    }
}

✅ Output: Thread is running...

The Supplier interface provides a value without taking any input. 


import java.util.function.Supplier;

public class SupplierExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Supplier<String> supplier = () -> "Hello, Supplier!";
        System.out.println(supplier.get());
    }
}

✅ Output: Hello, Supplier!

The Consumer interface consumes a value but does not return anything. 


import java.util.function.Consumer;

public class ConsumerExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Consumer<String> consumer = msg -> System.out.println("Consumed: " + msg);
        consumer.accept("Hello, Consumer!");
    }
}

✅ Output: Consumed: Hello, Consumer!

The Function interface takes an input of type T and returns a result of type R. 


import java.util.function.Function;

public class FunctionExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Function<Integer, String> function = num -> "Number: " + num;
        System.out.println(function.apply(10));
    }
}

✅ Output: Number: 10

The Predicate interface takes an input and returns a boolean value. 


import java.util.function.Predicate;

public class PredicateExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Predicate<Integer> isEven = num -> num % 2 == 0;
        System.out.println(isEven.test(10)); // true
        System.out.println(isEven.test(5));  // false
    }
}

✅ Output: true and false

Yes, we can have methods with the same name in a class using Method Overloading and Method Overriding. However, certain cases will cause compilation errors.

📌 1. Method Overloading (Same Class, Different Parameters)

Methods with the same name but different parameter lists are allowed.


class Calculator {
    // Overloaded method with two int parameters
    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    // Overloaded method with three int parameters
    int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }

    // Overloaded method with double parameters
    double add(double a, double b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}

✅ Allowed because the parameter lists are different.

📌 2. Method Overriding (Subclass Redefining Parent Class Method)

A subclass can redefine a method from the parent class.


class Parent {
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Parent class method");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Child class method");
    }
}

✅ Allowed because the method is being redefined in a subclass.

❌ 3. Same Method Signature with Different Return Types

Methods cannot have the same name and parameters but different return types.


class Example {
    int method() { return 5; }
    double method() { return 5.5; }  // ❌ Compilation Error! Same signature.
}

❌ Not Allowed because return type alone does not differentiate methods.

✅ Conclusion

We CAN have the same method name using method overloading and method overriding, but CANNOT have the same signature with different return types in the same class.

In Java, if a class does not explicitly define a constructor, the compiler automatically provides a default constructor.

📌 1. Default Constructor by Compiler

Even if no constructor is defined, the Java compiler generates a default constructor with no arguments. 


class Example {
    // No explicit constructor
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Example obj = new Example(); // Works because Java provides a default constructor
        System.out.println("Object created successfully!");
    }
}

The default constructor initializes the object without any custom logic.

📌 2. Using Reflection API

Objects can also be created using reflection, even if no constructor is defined explicitly.


import java.lang.reflect.Constructor;

class Sample {
    // No explicit constructor
}

public class ReflectionExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Constructor constructor = Sample.class.getDeclaredConstructor();
        Sample obj = constructor.newInstance();
        System.out.println("Object created using reflection!");
    }
}
📌 3. Using clone() Method

Objects can be created without calling a constructor using cloning.


class CloneExample implements Cloneable {
    @Override
    protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        return super.clone();
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        CloneExample obj1 = new CloneExample();
        CloneExample obj2 = (CloneExample) obj1.clone();
        System.out.println("Object created using clone method!");
    }
}
📌 4. Using Serialization & Deserialization

Objects can be created without calling a constructor through deserialization.


import java.io.*;

class SerializedExample implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
}

public class SerializationTest {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        SerializedExample obj1 = new SerializedExample();
        
        // Serialize
        ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("object.dat"));
        out.writeObject(obj1);
        out.close();
        
        // Deserialize
        ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream("object.dat"));
        SerializedExample obj2 = (SerializedExample) in.readObject();
        in.close();
        
        System.out.println("Object created using serialization!");
    }
}
✅ Conclusion

Even if a class does not explicitly define a constructor, Java provides ways to create objects through default constructors, reflection, cloning, and serialization. Understanding these methods helps in advanced Java programming and optimizations.

Both Comparable and Comparator are used for sorting objects, but they have key differences.

📌 Comparable (Natural Ordering)

Comparable is used to define the natural sorting order of objects. It is implemented within the class itself.


import java.util.*;

class Employee implements Comparable {
    int id;
    String name;
    
    public Employee(int id, String name) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
    }
    
    @Override
    public int compareTo(Employee e) {
        return this.id - e.id; // Sorting by ID (Ascending Order)
    }
    
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return id + " - " + name;
    }
}

public class ComparableExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List employees = new ArrayList<>();
        employees.add(new Employee(3, "Alice"));
        employees.add(new Employee(1, "Bob"));
        employees.add(new Employee(2, "Charlie"));

        Collections.sort(employees);
        System.out.println(employees); // Sorted by ID
    }
}

✅ Uses compareTo() method and modifies the class itself.

📌 Comparator (Custom Ordering)

Comparator is used when we want multiple sorting criteria without modifying the class.


import java.util.*;

class Employee {
    int id;
    String name;
    
    public Employee(int id, String name) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
    }
    
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return id + " - " + name;
    }
}

class NameComparator implements Comparator {
    @Override
    public int compare(Employee e1, Employee e2) {
        return e1.name.compareTo(e2.name); // Sorting by Name (Alphabetical Order)
    }
}

public class ComparatorExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List employees = new ArrayList<>();
        employees.add(new Employee(3, "Alice"));
        employees.add(new Employee(1, "Bob"));
        employees.add(new Employee(2, "Charlie"));

        Collections.sort(employees, new NameComparator());
        System.out.println(employees); // Sorted by Name
    }
}

✅ Uses a separate Comparator class and can define multiple sorting criteria.

🔍 Key Differences
  • Comparable: Defined inside the class using compareTo(). Affects natural ordering.
  • Comparator: Defined externally using compare(). Allows multiple sorting options.
  • Flexibility: Comparator is more flexible as it does not modify the class.

Both .equals() and == are used for comparison, but they serve different purposes.

📌 1. Using == (Reference Comparison)

The == operator compares memory addresses, checking if two references point to the same object.


String str1 = new String("Hello");
String str2 = new String("Hello");
System.out.println(str1 == str2); // false (Different memory locations)

Even though both strings have the same content, == returns false because they are different objects in memory.

📌 2. Using .equals() (Content Comparison)

The .equals() method checks the actual content of objects.


String str1 = new String("Hello");
String str2 = new String("Hello");
System.out.println(str1.equals(str2)); // true (Same content)

Since .equals() is overridden in the String class, it compares values instead of references.

📌 3. Behavior in Custom Objects

For custom objects, the default .equals() behaves like == unless overridden. 


class Person {
    String name;
    Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

Person p1 = new Person("Alice");
Person p2 = new Person("Alice");
System.out.println(p1.equals(p2)); // false (No override, behaves like ==)

To compare based on values, override equals() in the class.

✅ Conclusion
  • == checks if two references point to the same object.
  • .equals() checks if two objects have the same content (when properly overridden).

The Cloneable interface in Java is used to create exact copies (clones) of objects. It is a marker interface (i.e., it has no methods) that indicates the implementing class supports cloning using the clone() method of Object.

📌 1. Key Points About Cloneable
  • It is a marker interface (has no methods).
  • Classes implementing Cloneable must override clone() from Object.
  • Default cloning is shallow copy unless explicitly deep-cloned.
  • Without implementing Cloneable, calling clone() will throw CloneNotSupportedException.
📌 2. Example of Shallow Cloning

class Address {
    String city;
    Address(String city) {
        this.city = city;
    }
}

class Person implements Cloneable {
    String name;
    Address address;

    Person(String name, Address address) {
        this.name = name;
        this.address = address;
    }

    @Override
    protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        return super.clone(); // Shallow copy
    }
}

public class CloneExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        Address address = new Address("New York");
        Person p1 = new Person("John", address);
        Person p2 = (Person) p1.clone();

        p2.name = "Mike";
        p2.address.city = "Los Angeles"; // Changes in cloned object reflect in original

        System.out.println(p1.name + " - " + p1.address.city); // Output: John - Los Angeles
    }
}
📌 3. Example of Deep Cloning

class Address implements Cloneable {
    String city;
    Address(String city) {
        this.city = city;
    }
    @Override
    protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        return new Address(this.city); // Deep copy
    }
}

class Person implements Cloneable {
    String name;
    Address address;

    Person(String name, Address address) {
        this.name = name;
        this.address = address;
    }

    @Override
    protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        Person cloned = (Person) super.clone();
        cloned.address = (Address) address.clone(); // Deep copy
        return cloned;
    }
}
✅ Conclusion

The Cloneable interface allows object cloning in Java. By default, cloning is shallow, meaning changes in cloned objects affect the original. For deep cloning, each reference-type field must also implement Cloneable and override clone() accordingly.

A marker interface is an interface that has no methods or fields. It is used to provide metadata about a class to the JVM or frameworks.

  • Provides Metadata → Tells JVM that a class has a special behavior.
  • Used for Type Checking → Allows checking if an object belongs to a specific category.
  • Helps in Enforcing Contracts → Java APIs rely on marker interfaces for additional functionalities.

import java.io.Serializable;

class Employee implements Serializable {
    private String name;
    private int id;
    
    public Employee(String name, int id) {
        this.name = name;
        this.id = id;
    }
}

📌 Serializable ensures that the object can be converted into a byte stream for storage or transmission.

class Person implements Cloneable {
    String name;
    Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
    
    @Override
    protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        return super.clone();
    }
}

public class CloneableExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        Person p1 = new Person("John");
        Person p2 = (Person) p1.clone();
        System.out.println("Cloned Person: " + p2.name);
    }
}

📌 Cloneable ensures that the object can be cloned using clone() method.

interface Special {}

class CustomClass implements Special {
    void display() {
        System.out.println("This is a special class!");
    }
}

public class CustomMarkerExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CustomClass obj = new CustomClass();
        if (obj instanceof Special) {
            obj.display();
        }
    }
}

📌 The class is marked as Special, allowing us to perform type checks at runtime.

Annotations are preferred over marker interfaces as they provide more flexibility.

@interface Special {}

@Special
class AnnotatedClass {
    void show() {
        System.out.println("This class is marked as Special!");
    }
}

📌 Annotations offer additional metadata and customization, whereas marker interfaces act only as tags.

A Primary Key is a unique identifier for a record in a table. It ensures that no duplicate values exist and that the column cannot be NULL.

📌 Example:

CREATE TABLE Employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100),
    department VARCHAR(50)
);

Here, employee_id is the primary key, ensuring uniqueness.

A Foreign Key is a column that establishes a relationship between two tables by referring to a Primary Key in another table.

📌 Example:

CREATE TABLE Departments (
    department_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    department_name VARCHAR(50)
);

CREATE TABLE Employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100),
    department_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (department_id) REFERENCES Departments(department_id)
);

Here, department_id in the Employees table is a Foreign Key referring to the Primary Key in the Departments table.

Aspect Primary Key Foreign Key
Uniqueness Must be unique Can have duplicate values
NULL Values Cannot be NULL Can be NULL
Table Relationship Defines a unique identifier for a table Links two tables together
Number of Keys One per table Can have multiple foreign keys

No, HashMap is **not thread-safe** and can cause issues in a multithreaded environment.

If multiple threads modify a HashMap concurrently, it can lead to:

  • **Data corruption**
  • **Infinite loops (in Java 7 due to resize issues)**
  • **Unexpected behavior**

📌 Example of Failure:

import java.util.HashMap;

public class HashMapMultiThreadExample {
    static HashMap map = new HashMap<>();

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
                map.put(i, "Value" + i);
            }
        });

        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
                map.get(i);
            }
        });

        t1.start();
        t2.start();
    }
}

🔴 This may lead to **ConcurrentModificationException** or incorrect results.

There are **better alternatives** to using HashMap in a multithreaded environment:

✅ 1. Using Collections.synchronizedMap()

import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class SynchronizedMapExample {
    static Map map = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        map.put(1, "One");
        map.put(2, "Two");
    }
}

⚠️ **Limitations**: Only synchronizes method calls, but iteration still needs explicit synchronization.

✅ 2. Using ConcurrentHashMap

import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

public class ConcurrentHashMapExample {
    static ConcurrentHashMap map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        map.put(1, "One");
        map.put(2, "Two");
    }
}

✔️ **Best option for multi-threading** because it provides **better performance**.

Aspect HashMap ConcurrentHashMap
Thread Safety Not thread-safe Thread-safe
Performance Fast (Single-threaded) Fast (Multiple threads)
Synchronization Not synchronized Uses segments to reduce lock contention
Usage Best for single-threaded applications Best for multi-threaded environments

✅ Yes, Spring Boot is multi-threaded. It can handle multiple requests concurrently using a thread pool.

  • Spring Boot Web Applications: Uses Tomcat's thread pool (default 200 threads).
  • Asynchronous Execution: Uses @Async to run tasks in separate threads.
  • Parallel Processing: Uses ExecutorService or ForkJoinPool. 


@RestController
public class MultiThreadController {
    @GetMapping("/process")
    public String process() throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(3000); // Simulating time-consuming task
        return "Request handled by: " + Thread.currentThread().getName();
    }
}

📌 Different requests will be handled by different threads.


@Service
public class AsyncService {
    @Async
    public CompletableFuture asyncMethod() throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(2000);
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture("Async execution: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}

📌 This method will run in a separate thread.


@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class ThreadPoolConfig {
    @Bean
    public Executor asyncExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        executor.setCorePoolSize(10);
        executor.setMaxPoolSize(50);
        executor.setQueueCapacity(100);
        executor.initialize();
        return executor;
    }
}

📌 This configures a custom thread pool for async execution.

ConcurrentHashMap is a thread-safe implementation of HashMap that allows multiple threads to read and write without locking the entire map.

📌 Key Features:
  • Uses segment-based locking (in Java 7) and bucket-level locking (in Java 8).
  • Does not allow null keys or values.
  • Performs better than synchronized HashMap.

import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

public class ConcurrentHashMapExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ConcurrentHashMap map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        map.put(1, "Java");
        map.put(2, "Spring");
        System.out.println(map.get(1));
    }
}

CopyOnWriteArrayList is a thread-safe alternative to ArrayList where modifications create a new copy of the underlying array.

📌 Key Features:
  • Uses a copy-on-write mechanism.
  • Good for read-heavy operations, as reads don’t require synchronization.
  • Modifications are costly since they create a new array.

import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;

public class CopyOnWriteArrayListExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CopyOnWriteArrayList list = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
        list.add("Java");
        list.add("Spring");
        System.out.println(list);
    }
}

ConcurrentLinkedQueue is a non-blocking queue based on linked nodes.

📌 Key Features:
  • Uses lock-free algorithm for fast concurrent access.
  • Ideal for producer-consumer scenarios.
  • Uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap) for thread safety.

import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedQueue;

public class ConcurrentLinkedQueueExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ConcurrentLinkedQueue queue = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
        queue.add("Task1");
        queue.add("Task2");
        System.out.println(queue.poll());
    }
}

JWT (JSON Web Token) is an open standard (RFC 7519) for securely transmitting information between parties as a JSON object. It is mainly used for **authentication and authorization**.

✅ Use Cases
  • 🔐 Secure user authentication (OAuth2, OpenID Connect)
  • 📜 Information exchange between microservices
  • ⏳ Stateless session management

A JWT consists of **three parts**, separated by dots (`.`):

header.payload.signature
📌 1. Header

The header contains metadata like type and algorithm.

{
  "alg": "HS256",
  "typ": "JWT"
}
📌 2. Payload (Claims)

Contains the user information (claims).

{
  "sub": "1234567890",
  "name": "John Doe",
  "iat": 1711907300,
  "exp": 1711910900
}
📌 3. Signature

The signature ensures integrity of the token.

HMACSHA256(
  base64UrlEncode(header) + "." + base64UrlEncode(payload),
  secret-key
)

📌 Step-by-Step Flow
  1. 🔑 User logs in and provides credentials.
  2. ✅ Server validates credentials and generates a JWT.
  3. 📩 Server sends the JWT back to the client.
  4. 🔁 Client includes the JWT in **Authorization** header.
  5. 🛡️ Server verifies JWT signature and processes request.
📌 Example API Request
GET /api/data
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

✅ Pros of JWT
  • 🔹 **Stateless** – No need to store sessions on the server.
  • 🔹 **Compact** – Small and easy to transmit over HTTP headers.
  • 🔹 **Secure** – Signed to prevent tampering.
❌ Cons of JWT
  • ⚠️ **Cannot be invalidated** unless using a **token blacklist**.
  • ⚠️ **Payload is readable** if not encrypted (use HTTPS!).
  • ⚠️ **Longer tokens** can increase request size.

🚀 `map()` is used for **transformation**. It applies a function to each element and returns a new stream.

📝 Example:

Transform a list of names to uppercase using `map()`:


import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class MapExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List names = List.of("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie");

        List upperCaseNames = names.stream()
                                           .map(String::toUpperCase)  // Convert each name to uppercase
                                           .collect(Collectors.toList());

        System.out.println(upperCaseNames); // Output: [ALICE, BOB, CHARLIE]
    }
}

✅ `map()` maintains a one-to-one mapping (each element is transformed individually).

🚀 `flatMap()` is used to **flatten nested structures** (like List of Lists) into a single stream.

📝 Example:

Flatten a list of lists into a single list:


import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class FlatMapExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List> nestedList = List.of(
                List.of("Java", "Python"),
                List.of("C++", "Go"),
                List.of("Rust", "Kotlin")
        );

        List flatList = nestedList.stream()
                                          .flatMap(List::stream) // Flatten the lists
                                          .collect(Collectors.toList());

        System.out.println(flatList); // Output: [Java, Python, C++, Go, Rust, Kotlin]
    }
}

✅ `flatMap()` is useful when dealing with nested collections (removes extra layers).

Feature map() flatMap()
Purpose Transforms elements individually. Flattens and transforms nested structures.
Output Returns a **Stream of objects**. Returns a **flattened Stream**.
Use Case When transformation is one-to-one. When dealing with nested lists or optional values.
Example Convert a list of strings to uppercase. Flatten a list of lists into a single list.

📌 Synchronous communication means one service calls another and waits for a response.

✅ Using REST API (HTTP Call)

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/order")
public class OrderController {
    private final RestTemplate restTemplate;

    @Autowired
    public OrderController(RestTemplate restTemplate) {
        this.restTemplate = restTemplate;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{orderId}")
    public Order getOrder(@PathVariable String orderId) {
        Customer customer = restTemplate.getForObject("http://customer-service/customers/" + orderId, Customer.class);
        return new Order(orderId, customer);
    }
}

📝 Uses `RestTemplate` or `WebClient` to make API calls between services.

✅ Using gRPC (Binary Protocol, Faster than REST)

// gRPC Interface Definition
service CustomerService {
    rpc GetCustomer (CustomerRequest) returns (CustomerResponse);
}

📝 gRPC is more efficient than REST as it uses Protocol Buffers.

📌 Asynchronous communication allows services to send messages without waiting for a response.

✅ Using RabbitMQ (Message Queue)

@Component
public class OrderEventProducer {
    private final RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate;

    @Autowired
    public OrderEventProducer(RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate) {
        this.rabbitTemplate = rabbitTemplate;
    }

    public void sendOrderEvent(Order order) {
        rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend("order.queue", order);
    }
}

📝 Messages are queued and processed asynchronously.

✅ Using Kafka (Event Streaming)

@Component
public class OrderEventProducer {
    private final KafkaTemplate kafkaTemplate;

    @Autowired
    public OrderEventProducer(KafkaTemplate kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    public void publishOrderEvent(Order order) {
        kafkaTemplate.send("order-events", order);
    }
}

📝 Kafka is useful for event-driven architectures.

📌 Service Discovery allows microservices to dynamically find each other.

✅ Eureka Client Example

@LoadBalanced
@Bean
public RestTemplate restTemplate() {
    return new RestTemplate();
}

📝 `@LoadBalanced` helps to communicate with microservices without hardcoding URLs.

In Java, some collections maintain a sorted order. Below are the key ones:

📌 1. TreeSet (Sorted Set)

Maintains elements in **ascending order** using a **Red-Black Tree**. It does not allow duplicates.


import java.util.TreeSet;

public class TreeSetExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TreeSet numbers = new TreeSet<>();
        numbers.add(50);
        numbers.add(10);
        numbers.add(30);
        numbers.add(20);

        System.out.println(numbers); // Output: [10, 20, 30, 50] (Sorted order)
    }
}
📌 2. TreeMap (Sorted Map)

Maintains **keys in sorted order** using a **Red-Black Tree**.


import java.util.TreeMap;

public class TreeMapExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TreeMap scores = new TreeMap<>();
        scores.put("Alice", 90);
        scores.put("Bob", 85);
        scores.put("Charlie", 95);

        System.out.println(scores); // Output: {Alice=90, Bob=85, Charlie=95} (Keys sorted)
    }
}
📌 3. PriorityQueue (Sorted Queue)

Uses **Min-Heap** where the smallest element is retrieved first.


import java.util.PriorityQueue;

public class PriorityQueueExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PriorityQueue pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
        pq.add(50);
        pq.add(10);
        pq.add(30);
        pq.add(20);

        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            System.out.print(pq.poll() + " "); // Output: 10 20 30 50 (Ascending order)
        }
    }
}
⚠️ LinkedHashMap - Maintains Insertion Order, Not Sorted

Unlike `TreeMap`, it does **not** sort elements but **preserves insertion order**.


import java.util.LinkedHashMap;

public class LinkedHashMapExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedHashMap map = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        map.put("Zebra", 1);
        map.put("Apple", 2);
        map.put("Mango", 3);

        System.out.println(map); // Output: {Zebra=1, Apple=2, Mango=3} (Insertion order)
    }
}
✅ Summary Table
Collection Sorted? Maintains Order? Allows Duplicates?
TreeSet ✅ Yes (Ascending) ❌ No ❌ No
TreeMap ✅ Yes (Keys Sorted) ❌ No ✅ Yes (Unique Keys)
PriorityQueue ✅ Yes (Min-Heap) ❌ No ✅ Yes
LinkedHashMap ❌ No (Insertion Order) ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
🔍 Best Choice for Different Use Cases
  • ✔ **Use `TreeSet`** if you need a unique, sorted collection.
  • ✔ **Use `TreeMap`** if you need a sorted key-value store.
  • ✔ **Use `PriorityQueue`** if you need a priority-based queue.
  • ✔ **Use `LinkedHashMap`** if you only care about insertion order.

Java provides several thread-safe collections that can be used in a **multi-threaded environment**. These collections prevent concurrency issues and ensure safe access.

📌 1. Collections.synchronizedXXX() (Wrapper Methods)

The **Collections class** provides methods to make existing collections thread-safe.


import java.util.*;

public class SynchronizedListExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List list = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        list.add("A");
        list.add("B");
        list.add("C");

        synchronized (list) { // External synchronization is needed for iteration
            for (String s : list) {
                System.out.println(s);
            }
        }
    }
}

Similar methods:

  • Collections.synchronizedList(List list)
  • Collections.synchronizedSet(Set set)
  • Collections.synchronizedMap(Map map)
📌 2. CopyOnWriteArrayList (Thread-Safe List)

Creates a copy of the list on every modification, avoiding `ConcurrentModificationException`.


import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;

public class CopyOnWriteArrayListExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CopyOnWriteArrayList list = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
        list.add("A");
        list.add("B");
        list.add("C");

        for (String s : list) {
            list.add("D"); // No ConcurrentModificationException
        }

        System.out.println(list); // Output: [A, B, C, D, D, D]
    }
}
📌 3. ConcurrentHashMap (Thread-Safe Map)

Uses segment-based locking to allow **concurrent reads and writes**.


import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

public class ConcurrentHashMapExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ConcurrentHashMap map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        map.put(1, "Java");
        map.put(2, "Spring");
        map.put(3, "Hibernate");

        map.forEach((key, value) -> System.out.println(key + " -> " + value));
    }
}
📌 4. ConcurrentLinkedQueue (Thread-Safe Queue)

A **lock-free queue** that allows high-performance concurrent access.


import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedQueue;

public class ConcurrentQueueExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ConcurrentLinkedQueue queue = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
        queue.offer("One");
        queue.offer("Two");

        System.out.println(queue.poll()); // Output: One
        System.out.println(queue.poll()); // Output: Two
    }
}
📌 5. BlockingQueue (Thread-Safe Queue for Producer-Consumer)

Blocks if the queue is full or empty, making it useful for **producer-consumer problems**.


import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue;

public class BlockingQueueExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        BlockingQueue queue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(2);
        queue.put("A");
        queue.put("B");

        System.out.println(queue.take()); // Output: A
        System.out.println(queue.take()); // Output: B
    }
}
⚠️ Non-Thread-Safe Collections

The following collections are **NOT thread-safe** unless explicitly synchronized:

  • ArrayList
  • HashMap
  • HashSet
  • LinkedList
✅ Summary Table
Collection Type Thread-Safe Version
List Collections.synchronizedList(), CopyOnWriteArrayList
Set Collections.synchronizedSet(), ConcurrentSkipListSet
Map Collections.synchronizedMap(), ConcurrentHashMap
Queue ConcurrentLinkedQueue, BlockingQueue
🔍 Best Choice for Different Use Cases
  • ✔ **Use `CopyOnWriteArrayList`** when iteration is more frequent than modification.
  • ✔ **Use `ConcurrentHashMap`** when you need thread-safe key-value storage.
  • ✔ **Use `BlockingQueue`** for producer-consumer scenarios.

Cloning in Java is used to create a copy of an object. It can be done in two ways:

📌 1. Shallow Cloning

- In **shallow cloning**, a new object is created, but its fields **reference the same objects** as the original. - Changes in referenced objects affect both original and cloned objects. 


class Address implements Cloneable {
    String city;
    
    Address(String city) {
        this.city = city;
    }

    @Override
    protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        return super.clone(); // Performs shallow copy
    }
}

class Person implements Cloneable {
    String name;
    Address address;

    Person(String name, Address address) {
        this.name = name;
        this.address = address;
    }

    @Override
    protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        return super.clone(); // Performs shallow copy
    }
}

public class ShallowCloneExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        Address address = new Address("New York");
        Person p1 = new Person("John", address);
        Person p2 = (Person) p1.clone(); // Shallow copy

        System.out.println("Before Modification: " + p2.address.city); // Output: New York

        p1.address.city = "Los Angeles"; // Changing original object reference

        System.out.println("After Modification: " + p2.address.city); // Output: Los Angeles (changes in both)
    }
}
⚠️ Issue with Shallow Copy

If the cloned object has references to other objects, both original and cloned objects **share** the same references. This can lead to unexpected modifications.

📌 2. Deep Cloning

- In **deep cloning**, a completely new object is created along with copies of all referenced objects. - The original and cloned objects are fully independent. 


class Address implements Cloneable {
    String city;
    
    Address(String city) {
        this.city = city;
    }

    @Override
    protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        return new Address(this.city); // Creates new object
    }
}

class Person implements Cloneable {
    String name;
    Address address;

    Person(String name, Address address) {
        this.name = name;
        this.address = address;
    }

    @Override
    protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        Person clonedPerson = (Person) super.clone();
        clonedPerson.address = (Address) address.clone(); // Deep Copy
        return clonedPerson;
    }
}

public class DeepCloneExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        Address address = new Address("New York");
        Person p1 = new Person("John", address);
        Person p2 = (Person) p1.clone(); // Deep copy

        System.out.println("Before Modification: " + p2.address.city); // Output: New York

        p1.address.city = "Los Angeles"; // Changing original object reference

        System.out.println("After Modification: " + p2.address.city); // Output: New York (independent copy)
    }
}
✅ Key Differences
Feature Shallow Copy Deep Copy
Copies primitive fields ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Copies reference fields ❌ No (Shares references) ✅ Yes (Creates new objects)
Objects are independent? ❌ No ✅ Yes
Changes in original reflect in cloned? ✅ Yes ❌ No
🔍 When to Use?
  • ✔ Use **shallow cloning** when references should be shared.
  • ✔ Use **deep cloning** when each object should be **fully independent**.
  • ✔ If cloning is required, consider **serialization-based deep copy** for complex objects.

Stereotype Annotations in Spring are **meta-annotations** used to define Spring-managed beans automatically. They help categorize different types of components in a Spring application.

📌 1. @Component (Generic Bean)

- Marks a class as a Spring-managed component. - Used for general-purpose beans that don't fit into a specific layer. 


@Component
public class MyComponent {
    public void execute() {
        System.out.println("Executing Component");
    }
}
📌 2. @Service (Business Logic Layer)

- Specialized version of @Component used for **business logic**. - It improves readability and helps indicate service classes. 


@Service
public class UserService {
    public String getUser() {
        return "John Doe";
    }
}
📌 3. @Repository (Data Access Layer)

- Marks a class as a **DAO (Data Access Object)**. - Provides exception translation for database-related operations. 


@Repository
public class UserRepository {
    public List getUsers() {
        return List.of("Alice", "Bob");
    }
}
📌 4. @Controller (Web Layer)

- Used in **Spring MVC** to mark a class as a controller. - Handles web requests and returns **view responses**. 


@Controller
public class HomeController {
    @GetMapping("/")
    public String home() {
        return "index";
    }
}
📌 5. @RestController (REST API Controller)

- Specialized version of @Controller for REST APIs. - Combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. 


@RestController
public class ApiController {
    @GetMapping("/user")
    public String getUser() {
        return "John Doe";
    }
}
✅ Comparison of Stereotype Annotations
Annotation Purpose Layer
@Component Generic Spring Bean Any Layer
@Service Business Logic Service Layer
@Repository Data Access Object Persistence Layer
@Controller Handles Web Requests Web Layer (MVC)
@RestController REST API Controller Web Layer (REST)
⚠️ Important Notes
  • ✔ All these annotations are **detected by Spring's Component Scanning**.
  • ✔ @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody.
  • ✔ @Repository enables **Spring Data Exception Translation**.
  • ✔ @Service improves **readability and business logic separation**.

In Spring Framework, there are multiple ways to manage transactions. The main methods are **Declarative Transaction Management** and **Programmatic Transaction Management**.

📌 1. Declarative Transaction Management (Recommended)

- Uses **Spring AOP and @Transactional** annotation. - No need to manually begin, commit, or rollback transactions. 


@Service
public class UserService {

    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;

    @Transactional
    public void createUser(User user) {
        userRepository.save(user);
        // Any runtime exception here will cause rollback
    }
}

✔ Advantages: Simple and less boilerplate code.

❌ Disadvantages: Cannot handle fine-grained transaction control.

📌 2. Programmatic Transaction Management

- Manages transactions manually using **TransactionTemplate** or **PlatformTransactionManager**. - Provides fine-grained transaction control.

🔹 Using TransactionTemplate

@Service
public class UserService {

    @Autowired
    private TransactionTemplate transactionTemplate;

    public void createUser(User user) {
        transactionTemplate.execute(status -> {
            userRepository.save(user);
            return null;
        });
    }
}
🔹 Using PlatformTransactionManager

@Service
public class UserService {

    @Autowired
    private PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager;

    public void createUser(User user) {
        DefaultTransactionDefinition def = new DefaultTransactionDefinition();
        TransactionStatus status = transactionManager.getTransaction(def);
        try {
            userRepository.save(user);
            transactionManager.commit(status);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            transactionManager.rollback(status);
        }
    }
}

✔ Advantages: More control over transactions.

❌ Disadvantages: More complex and requires manual handling.

📌 3. XML-Based Transaction Management

- Uses **XML configuration** instead of annotations. 


<tx:advice id="txAdvice" transaction-manager="transactionManager">
    <tx:attributes>
        <tx:method name="createUser" propagation="REQUIRED"/>
    </tx:attributes>
</tx:advice>

✔ Advantages: Useful for legacy applications.

❌ Disadvantages: XML configuration is verbose.

✅ Comparison of Transaction Management Approaches
Method Type Pros Cons
@Transactional Declarative Simple, less code Less control
TransactionTemplate Programmatic Fine-grained control More code
PlatformTransactionManager Programmatic Full control Complex
XML-Based Declarative Good for legacy Verbose
⚠️ Important Notes
  • ✔ **@Transactional** works only with public methods.
  • ✔ Rollback happens only for **unchecked exceptions** by default.
  • ✔ Programmatic transactions provide more flexibility but require manual control.

Atomic Variables in Java are part of the java.util.concurrent.atomic package. They provide **lock-free, thread-safe** operations for variables like integers, booleans, and references using **Compare-And-Swap (CAS)** mechanism.

📌 Why Use Atomic Variables?
  • Provides **thread-safe updates** without using synchronization.
  • **Better performance** than `synchronized` for simple operations.
  • Avoids issues like race conditions in multithreading.
📌 Types of Atomic Variables
  • AtomicInteger - For atomic integer operations.
  • AtomicLong - For atomic long operations.
  • AtomicBoolean - For atomic boolean values.
  • AtomicReference<T> - For atomic reference updates.
📌 Example: Using AtomicInteger

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class AtomicExample {
    private static AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> count.incrementAndGet()); // Atomic increment
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> count.incrementAndGet());

        t1.start();
        t2.start();

        try {
            t1.join();
            t2.join();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            e.printStackTrace();
        }

        System.out.println("Final Count: " + count.get()); // Output: 2
    }
}
📌 Compare-And-Swap (CAS) Mechanism

Atomic variables use **CAS (Compare-And-Swap)** instead of locks. This prevents thread contention: 


boolean updated = count.compareAndSet(0, 10); // If count == 0, set to 10
System.out.println(updated); // true if update successful
📌 When to Use Atomic Variables?
  • For **simple operations** like counters and flags.
  • When **high performance** is required.
  • If using **synchronized is too expensive** due to contention.
🔹 Summary Table
Atomic Type Usage
AtomicInteger Thread-safe integer operations.
AtomicLong Thread-safe long operations.
AtomicBoolean Thread-safe boolean updates.
AtomicReference<T> Thread-safe object references.
✅ Key Takeaways
  • Atomic variables use **lock-free, non-blocking** operations.
  • Best suited for **highly concurrent** applications.
  • For complex cases, **synchronization or locks** might still be required.

OAuth 2.0 (Open Authorization) is an **authorization framework** that allows secure access to resources without exposing user credentials. It is commonly used for **third-party access** to APIs like Google, Facebook, and GitHub.

📌 Key Components of OAuth 2.0
  • Resource Owner: The user who owns the data.
  • Client: The application requesting access.
  • Authorization Server: Issues access tokens after authentication.
  • Resource Server: Hosts protected resources (e.g., APIs).
📌 OAuth 2.0 Workflow

1. The client requests access from the resource owner.
2. The resource owner grants permission.
3. The client sends the request to the authorization server.
4. The authorization server issues an access token.
5. The client uses the token to access the resource server.
📌 Types of OAuth 2.0 Authentication Flows
🔹 1. Authorization Code Flow (Most Secure) 🔹

The **Authorization Code Flow** is the most secure method, as the access token is not exposed to the frontend. 


1. User logs in and authorizes the app.
2. App receives an **Authorization Code**.
3. The backend exchanges the code for an **Access Token**.
4. The token is used to access protected resources.
🔹 2. Implicit Flow (For Frontend Apps) 🔹

Used in **client-side apps** (Single Page Applications - SPA). It is less secure since tokens are exposed in the URL. 


1. User logs in and authorizes the app.
2. The browser directly receives an **Access Token**.
3. The token is used for API requests.
🔹 3. Client Credentials Flow (Machine-to-Machine) 🔹

Used for **server-to-server** authentication where no user is involved (e.g., Microservices communication). 


1. The client authenticates with the authorization server.
2. The server issues an **Access Token**.
3. The token is used to access resources.
🔹 4. Password Credentials Flow (Legacy Approach) 🔹

Used in **trusted applications** where the client directly collects the user's **username & password**. 


1. The user provides credentials to the app.
2. The app exchanges credentials for an **Access Token**.
3. The token is used to access resources.
🔹 5. Device Authorization Flow (For IoT Devices) 🔹

Used for **devices without browsers** (e.g., Smart TVs, IoT devices). The user logs in on a different device. 


1. The device requests authorization.
2. The user logs in on another device and enters a code.
3. The server issues an **Access Token**.
4. The device uses the token for API requests.
📌 Example: OAuth 2.0 with Spring Boot

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {
    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.oauth2Login();
        return http.build();
    }
}
✅ Summary Table
Flow Use Case Security Level
Authorization Code Web apps, secure login 🔒 High
Implicit SPA (Client-side apps) ⚠️ Low (Token in URL)
Client Credentials Machine-to-Machine 🔒 High
Password Credentials Trusted legacy apps ⚠️ Medium (Credentials shared)
Device Authorization IoT devices, TVs 🔒 High
✅ Key Takeaways
  • OAuth 2.0 enables **secure authorization** without sharing passwords.
  • **Authorization Code Flow** is the most secure and widely used.
  • Use **Client Credentials Flow** for microservices communication.
  • Implicit and Password Grant Types are **not recommended** for new applications.

Unit testing in Spring Boot ensures that individual components (such as services, controllers, and repositories) function correctly in isolation.

📌 Key Components of Unit Testing
  • JUnit 5 (Jupiter) - Testing framework.
  • Mockito - For mocking dependencies.
  • Spring Boot Test - Provides testing utilities.
  • AssertJ/Hamcrest - Assertion libraries for better test readability.
✅ 1. Setup Dependencies

Add the required dependencies in pom.xml:


<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.mockito</groupId>
        <artifactId>mockito-core</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
✅ 2. Testing a Service Layer with Mockito

Let's assume we have a simple **UserService** that fetches user data from a repository.


@Service
public class UserService {
    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }

    public User getUserById(Long id) {
        return userRepository.findById(id)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException("User not found"));
    }
}

Now, let's write a **unit test** for this service.


@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
public class UserServiceTest {

    @Mock
    private UserRepository userRepository;

    @InjectMocks
    private UserService userService;

    @Test
    void testGetUserById_Success() {
        User mockUser = new User(1L, "John Doe");
        when(userRepository.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(mockUser));

        User user = userService.getUserById(1L);

        assertNotNull(user);
        assertEquals("John Doe", user.getName());
        verify(userRepository, times(1)).findById(1L);
    }

    @Test
    void testGetUserById_NotFound() {
        when(userRepository.findById(2L)).thenReturn(Optional.empty());

        assertThrows(UserNotFoundException.class, () -> userService.getUserById(2L));
    }
}
✅ 3. Testing a Controller Layer with MockMvc

Let's assume we have a **UserController**.


@RestController
@RequestMapping("/users")
public class UserController {
    private final UserService userService;

    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUserById(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(userService.getUserById(id));
    }
}

Now, let's write a unit test using **MockMvc**.


@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)
public class UserControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    private MockMvc mockMvc;

    @MockBean
    private UserService userService;

    @Test
    void testGetUserById_Success() throws Exception {
        User mockUser = new User(1L, "John Doe");
        when(userService.getUserById(1L)).thenReturn(mockUser);

        mockMvc.perform(get("/users/1"))
                .andExpect(status().isOk())
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("John Doe"));
    }

    @Test
    void testGetUserById_NotFound() throws Exception {
        when(userService.getUserById(2L)).thenThrow(new UserNotFoundException("User not found"));

        mockMvc.perform(get("/users/2"))
                .andExpect(status().isNotFound());
    }
}
✅ Summary
  • Use **Mockito** to mock dependencies in service layer tests.
  • Use **MockMvc** to test controllers without starting the full application.
  • **Assertions** ensure expected outputs.
  • Test **exception handling** and edge cases.

Code Coverage is a metric that measures the percentage of your source code executed by your test cases. It helps ensure that critical parts of your application are tested and reduces the risk of undetected bugs.

📌 How Code Coverage Works

During test execution, a code coverage tool tracks which lines, branches, and paths in the source code are executed. The result is then displayed as a report, showing coverage percentages.

✅ Key Code Coverage Metrics
  • Line Coverage: Percentage of code lines executed by tests.
  • Branch Coverage: Ensures both if and else branches are tested.
  • Method Coverage: Ensures each method is executed at least once.
  • Path Coverage: Ensures all possible execution paths in a method are tested.
✅ Popular Code Coverage Tools
  • JaCoCo (Java Code Coverage): A widely used tool for Java applications.
  • Cobertura: Another Java coverage tool, but less popular than JaCoCo.
  • SonarQube: Provides advanced analysis, including code quality and coverage.
  • Emma: A lightweight coverage tool for Java.
✅ 1. Using JaCoCo in Spring Boot

Add the following dependency in pom.xml:


<plugin>
    <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
    <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>0.8.7</version>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>prepare-agent</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
        <execution>
            <id>report</id>
            <phase>verify</phase>
            <goals>
                <goal>report</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
✅ 2. Running JaCoCo

Execute the following command to generate the coverage report:


mvn clean test
mvn jacoco:report

The HTML report will be generated in target/site/jacoco/index.html.

✅ 3. Checking Code Coverage in IntelliJ IDEA
  1. Run tests with coverage: Ctrl + Shift + F10 → "Run with Coverage".
  2. View the coverage report in the **Coverage Tool Window**.
✅ 4. Enforcing Code Coverage in CI/CD

To fail the build if coverage is below a threshold, add this in pom.xml:


<configuration>
    <rules>
        <rule>
            <element>CLASS</element>
            <limits>
                <limit>
                    <counter>LINE</counter>
                    <value>COVEREDRATIO</value>
                    <minimum>0.80</minimum>
                </limit>
            </limits>
        </rule>
    </rules>
</configuration>
✅ Summary
  • Code coverage helps identify untested parts of the application.
  • JaCoCo is the most popular tool for Java applications.
  • Use coverage reports to improve test quality and prevent regressions.
  • Integrate coverage checks in CI/CD to maintain high test standards.

You can achieve this by using Java 8's Collectors.groupingBy() in combination with Collectors.counting() and Collectors.groupingBy() again.

📦 Employee Model

class Employee {
    private String name;
    private String gender;
    private String department;

    // Constructor, Getters, Setters
    public Employee(String name, String gender, String department) {
        this.name = name;
        this.gender = gender;
        this.department = department;
    }

    public String getGender() { return gender; }
    public String getDepartment() { return department; }
}
🧠 Java 8 Stream Code

List<Employee> employees = Arrays.asList(
    new Employee("John", "Male", "HR"),
    new Employee("Sara", "Female", "HR"),
    new Employee("Mike", "Male", "IT"),
    new Employee("Emma", "Female", "IT"),
    new Employee("Tom", "Male", "Finance")
);

Map<String, Map<String, Long>> genderCountByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::getDepartment,
        Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getGender, Collectors.counting())
    ));
🔍 Output Example

{
  HR={Male=1, Female=1},
  IT={Male=1, Female=1},
  Finance={Male=1}
}
✅ Explanation
  • groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment) groups by department
  • groupingBy(Employee::getGender) groups by gender inside each department
  • counting() counts the number of occurrences

✔️ This approach is clean and efficient for categorizing and counting data in complex nested structures using Streams.

NULL represents the absence of a value in SQL. Special care is needed to handle it correctly in conditions and functions.

🔍 1. Using IS NULL / IS NOT NULL

SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE department IS NULL;

Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL instead of = NULL (which won’t work).

🧪 2. Using COALESCE()

Returns the first non-null value among arguments.


SELECT name, COALESCE(mobile, 'N/A') AS phone_number
FROM users;
📦 3. Using NULLIF()

Returns NULL if the two arguments are equal, otherwise returns the first.


SELECT NULLIF(salary, 0) FROM employees;
🧮 4. Using CASE for Custom Handling

SELECT name,
  CASE
    WHEN bonus IS NULL THEN 'No Bonus'
    ELSE bonus
  END AS bonus_info
FROM employees;
💡 Pro Tips
  • NULL values don’t behave like normal values in comparisons.
  • NULL = NULL is FALSE, but IS NULL works.
  • Use COALESCE or CASE to provide defaults or alternative logic.

✅ Proper NULL handling ensures reliable query results and prevents logical bugs.

🔄 A subquery is a query nested inside another SQL query. A join is used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column.

📍 Subquery Example:

Get employees who earn more than the average salary:


SELECT name, salary 
FROM employees 
WHERE salary > (
    SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees
);
🔗 Join Example:

Get employee names and their department names:


SELECT e.name, d.department_name 
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;
🔍 Key Differences
  • Subqueries return single or multiple values and are often used in WHERE, HAVING, or FROM clauses.
  • Joins combine rows from multiple tables into a single result set.
  • Performance: Joins are generally faster than subqueries as they are optimized by the SQL engine.
  • Readability: Subqueries can make the query more modular or readable when filtering based on derived data.

💡 Use subqueries when you need intermediate calculations or filtering, and joins when combining data from related tables.

Idempotency ensures that processing the same message multiple times results in the same system state — avoiding duplicates and inconsistencies.

📌 Common Causes of Duplicate Messages
  • Kafka retries due to consumer failure
  • Network partitioning
  • Manual replay of messages
  • Consumer crash before acknowledging offset
✅ Idempotency Strategies
1. Use of Unique Message Keys / IDs

Each event/message should carry a unique identifier (e.g., eventId, orderId, etc.) generated by the producer. Consumers can track and ignore already processed events.

2. Idempotency Key Store (Persistence)

Maintain a datastore (Redis, DB, etc.) to track processed message IDs:

  • Check if eventId exists in the store
  • If exists → Skip processing
  • If not → Process and mark it as processed
3. Deduplication in Database

Use database-level constraints like unique indexes to ensure records are not inserted more than once.


CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  ...
);
4. Transactional Outbox Pattern

Instead of publishing Kafka messages directly, store them in an "outbox" table within the same DB transaction. Use a separate service to poll and publish those events to Kafka. Ensures atomicity.

5. Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS)

Kafka offers **EOS** for producers and Kafka Streams. Configure enable.idempotence=true in producers and use **transactional producers** to ensure message is published and consumed exactly once.

6. Consumer Offset Management

Always commit the offset after the successful processing of the message. This ensures a message is retried only if it wasn't fully processed.

🔐 Design Recommendations
  • Design consumer services to be stateless and idempotent
  • Use idempotent service logic (e.g., PUT/UPSERT operations)
  • Use message headers to pass metadata like correlationId
  • Enable retry mechanisms with backoff and dead-letter queues (DLQ)

🔁 Conclusion: Idempotency in Kafka is essential for data consistency. Combine Kafka configurations, stateless processing, and durable idempotency tracking mechanisms for robust design.

🔹 1. transient

transient variables are not serialized. When the object is deserialized, they will be initialized to their default values (e.g., null, 0, etc.).

🔹 2. static

static variables belong to the class, not the instance. So, they are not serialized. Their value comes from the current JVM, not from the serialized object.

🔹 3. final

final variables are serialized if they are not transient or static. They behave like normal instance variables.

📌 Example

import java.io.*;

class Person implements Serializable {
    private String name;
    private transient int age; // won't be serialized
    private static String type = "Human"; // not serialized
    private final String gender; // serialized

    public Person(String name, int age, String gender) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
        this.gender = gender;
    }
}
🔎 Summary
  • transient ❌ Not serialized
  • static ❌ Not serialized
  • final ✅ Serialized (unless static/transient)

🔸 Enum in JPA/Hibernate

JPA supports mapping enum types as fields in entities using the @Enumerated annotation. This helps Hibernate store the enum value in the database as either a String or an Ordinal (int).

💡 Usage
  • EnumType.STRING: Stores enum name like "ACTIVE"
  • EnumType.ORDINAL: Stores enum ordinal like 0, 1
✅ Recommended: EnumType.STRING

Using STRING is safer for versioning and readability. Changing the order of enum constants won't affect data.

📌 Example

public enum Status {
    ACTIVE,
    INACTIVE,
    DELETED
}

@Entity
public class User {
    @Id
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) // or EnumType.ORDINAL
    private Status status;
}
📌 SQL Output with STRING

-- For EnumType.STRING
INSERT INTO user (id, name, status) VALUES (1, 'John', 'ACTIVE');
📌 SQL Output with ORDINAL

-- For EnumType.ORDINAL
-- ACTIVE = 0, INACTIVE = 1, DELETED = 2
INSERT INTO user (id, name, status) VALUES (1, 'John', 0);
⚠️ Caution

Avoid EnumType.ORDINAL unless absolutely necessary. Changing enum order can corrupt your data mapping.

🔹 DELETE
  • Removes rows one at a time based on a condition (optional).
  • Can be rolled back (transaction-safe).
  • Triggers ON DELETE constraints or triggers if defined.
  • Slower compared to TRUNCATE for large tables.
  • You can use WHERE clause.
DELETE FROM employees WHERE department = 'HR';
🔹 TRUNCATE
  • Deletes all rows in a table instantly.
  • Cannot use WHERE clause.
  • Cannot be rolled back in most databases.
  • Does not fire triggers in many DBs.
  • Faster and uses fewer system & transaction log resources.
  • Resets identity (auto increment) in some DBs.
TRUNCATE TABLE employees;
📌 Summary Table
Aspect DELETE TRUNCATE
WHERE Clause Yes No
Rollback Yes No (usually)
Triggers Yes No (usually)
Speed Slower Faster
Reset Auto-Increment No Yes (depends on DB)

🔹 What is an Immutable Class?
  • An Immutable Class is a class whose state cannot be changed once it is created.
  • All fields are private and final.
  • No setters; fields are set via constructor only.
  • Any mutable objects must be deep copied during construction and when accessed via getters.
✅ Benefits of Immutable Classes
  • Thread-safe by default.
  • Safe to use in cache or shared environments.
  • Better for debugging and testing.
💡 Example: Immutable Class with Mutable Field
public final class Employee {

    private final String name;
    private final Date joiningDate;

    public Employee(String name, Date joiningDate) {
        this.name = name;
        // Defensive copy
        this.joiningDate = new Date(joiningDate.getTime());
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public Date getJoiningDate() {
        // Return defensive copy
        return new Date(joiningDate.getTime());
    }
}
⚠️ What Happens Without Defensive Copy?
  • If you return the actual Date/List/Map reference, its internal state can be modified from outside.
  • This breaks immutability.
💡 Example with List (Mutable)
public final class Department {

    private final List<String> employees;

    public Department(List<String> employees) {
        // Defensive copy
        this.employees = new ArrayList<>(employees);
    }

    public List<String> getEmployees() {
        // Defensive copy
        return new ArrayList<>(employees);
    }
}
✅ Good Practices
  • Use Collections.unmodifiableList() if deep copy is not needed.
  • Make class final to prevent inheritance.
  • Return defensive copies of mutable fields in getters.
🧠 Quick Recap
  • Immutable ≠ no mutable fields. It means mutable fields cannot be changed from outside.
  • Use defensive copies in constructor and getter.

📌 SQL Functions
  • Returns a single value (scalar) or a table.
  • Can be used in SELECT statements.
  • Must return a value using RETURN.
  • Cannot modify database state (usually no INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE).
  • Useful for reusable business logic in queries.
Example:
CREATE FUNCTION GetDiscount(@amount DECIMAL)
RETURNS DECIMAL
AS
BEGIN
    RETURN @amount * 0.10;
END;
📌 Stored Procedures
  • Performs one or more operations (including DML).
  • Can have input, output, and return parameters.
  • Used for complex logic with conditions, loops, and transactions.
  • Can be called explicitly using EXEC or CALL.
Example:
CREATE PROCEDURE UpdateSalary
  @empId INT,
  @increment DECIMAL
AS
BEGIN
  UPDATE Employee SET Salary = Salary + @increment WHERE Id = @empId;
END;
🔄 Key Differences
Feature Function Stored Procedure
Return Type Must return a value May or may not return a value
Usage in Queries Can be used in SELECT Cannot be used in SELECT
DML Operations Usually not allowed Allowed
Error Handling Limited Robust (Try-Catch)
Transactions No Yes
🧠 Conclusion
  • Use Functions for small calculations or logic in queries.
  • Use Stored Procedures for complex business operations and DB manipulations.

📌 String
  • Immutable – any modification creates a new object.
  • Stored in string pool (memory efficient).
  • Thread-safe due to immutability.
  • Slower in repeated modifications due to object creation.
String s1 = "Hello";
String s2 = s1.concat(" World"); // New object created
System.out.println(s2);
Common String methods:
  • length()
  • charAt(int index)
  • substring(int start, int end)
  • equals(Object obj)
  • indexOf(String str)
  • toUpperCase(), toLowerCase()
📌 StringBuilder
  • Mutable – changes apply to the same object.
  • Not synchronized – Not thread-safe.
  • Faster in single-threaded environments.
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("Hello");
sb.append(" World");
System.out.println(sb.toString());
Common StringBuilder methods:
  • append(String str)
  • insert(int offset, String str)
  • delete(int start, int end)
  • reverse()
  • replace(int start, int end, String str)
📌 StringBuffer
  • Mutable and Synchronized – thread-safe.
  • Slightly slower than StringBuilder due to synchronization.
  • Useful in multi-threaded scenarios.
StringBuffer sbf = new StringBuffer("Hello");
sbf.append(" World");
System.out.println(sbf);
Common StringBuffer methods:
  • append(String str)
  • insert(int offset, String str)
  • delete(int start, int end)
  • reverse()
  • capacity(), ensureCapacity(int min)
✅ Conclusion
Feature String StringBuilder StringBuffer
Mutable No Yes Yes
Thread-Safe Yes (due to immutability) No Yes
Performance Slow (many objects) Fast (single-threaded) Slower (due to sync)

📌 What is API Gateway?

API Gateway is a single entry point for all clients. It handles request routing, composition, security, monitoring, and more. In a microservice architecture, it hides service internals from clients.

📌 How does it know where to route?
  • Uses predefined routing configuration.
  • Can use service discovery (e.g., Eureka, Consul).
  • Can use static route mapping (host/path based).
  • Load balancing using Ribbon, Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, etc.
✅ Example with Spring Cloud Gateway
# application.yml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: user-service
          uri: lb://USER-SERVICE
          predicates:
            - Path=/user/**

        - id: order-service
          uri: lb://ORDER-SERVICE
          predicates:
            - Path=/order/**

🧠 The `lb://` prefix means it will use LoadBalancer to look up the actual service instance from service registry (like Eureka).

🔗 With Service Discovery (Eureka)
// Eureka Client in UserService
@EnableEurekaClient
@SpringBootApplication
public class UserServiceApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(UserServiceApplication.class, args);
    }
}

Now, Spring Cloud Gateway registers itself and looks up services from Eureka registry. Based on route paths, it knows which service to forward the request to.

🧭 Alternate Routing Strategies
  • Path-based routing: `/api/user/**` → User Service
  • Host-based routing: `user.api.com` → User Service
  • Header-based routing: If header = "X-Env: dev" → Dev service
  • Query param routing: `/search?type=order` → Order service
🔐 Other Features of Gateway
  • Authentication & Authorization
  • Rate Limiting
  • Circuit Breaker
  • Logging, Metrics, Monitoring
📦 Supported Gateways
  • Spring Cloud Gateway
  • Netflix Zuul (legacy)
  • NGINX / HAProxy
  • Amazon API Gateway
  • Kong, Apigee, Tyk

Problem: Move all 0s to the front of the array, keeping the relative order of non-zero elements.

Example:

Input:  [1, 0, 2, 0, 3, 4, 0, 5]
Output: [0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Solution:

public static int[] moveZerosToFront(int[] arr) {
    List<Integer> nonZeroList = new ArrayList<>();
    int zeroCount = 0;

    for (int num : arr) {
        if (num == 0) {
            zeroCount++;
        } else {
            nonZeroList.add(num);
        }
    }

    int[] result = new int[arr.length];

    for (int i = 0; i < zeroCount; i++) {
        result[i] = 0;
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < nonZeroList.size(); i++) {
        result[zeroCount + i] = nonZeroList.get(i);
    }

    return result;
}

Explanation:

  • First, count the number of zeros.
  • Collect non-zero values preserving order.
  • Create a new result array.
  • Fill zeros at the beginning, then copy non-zeros.

1. Predicate<T> — returns a boolean.

Predicate<String> isLong = str -> str.length() > 5;
System.out.println(isLong.test("Hello")); // false

2. Consumer<T> — takes input, returns nothing.

Consumer<String> printer = s -> System.out.println(s);
printer.accept("Hello Consumer");

3. Function<T, R> — takes input and returns result.

Function<String, Integer> toLength = s -> s.length();
System.out.println(toLength.apply("Java")); // 4

4. Supplier<T> — supplies a result of type T.

Supplier<String> randomUUID = () -> UUID.randomUUID().toString();
System.out.println(randomUUID.get());

5. UnaryOperator<T> — special case of Function: input and output types are same.

UnaryOperator<Integer> square = x -> x * x;
System.out.println(square.apply(5)); // 25

6. BinaryOperator<T> — takes 2 inputs of same type, returns same type.

BinaryOperator<Integer> add = (a, b) -> a + b;
System.out.println(add.apply(2, 3)); // 5

7. BiFunction<T, U, R> — takes two arguments, returns a result.

BiFunction<Integer, Integer, String> sumToStr = (a, b) -> "Sum is " + (a + b);
System.out.println(sumToStr.apply(2, 3));

8. BiPredicate<T, U> — takes two inputs, returns boolean.

BiPredicate<String, Integer> checker = (s, len) -> s.length() == len;
System.out.println(checker.test("Hello", 5)); // true

9. BiConsumer<T, U> — accepts two arguments and returns nothing.

BiConsumer<String, Integer> printer = (name, age) ->
    System.out.println(name + " is " + age + " years old");
printer.accept("Alice", 30);

10. IntFunction<R>, DoubleFunction<R>, LongFunction<R>

IntFunction<String> toHex = Integer::toHexString;
System.out.println(toHex.apply(255)); // ff

11. IntSupplier, LongSupplier, DoubleSupplier

IntSupplier random = () -> new Random().nextInt(10);
System.out.println(random.getAsInt());

12. IntPredicate, LongPredicate, DoublePredicate

IntPredicate isEven = x -> x % 2 == 0;
System.out.println(isEven.test(4)); // true

13. IntUnaryOperator, LongUnaryOperator, DoubleUnaryOperator

IntUnaryOperator triple = x -> x * 3;
System.out.println(triple.applyAsInt(3)); // 9

14. BooleanSupplier

BooleanSupplier condition = () -> 5 > 3;
System.out.println(condition.getAsBoolean()); // true

Note:

  • All these are part of java.util.function package.
  • They support lambda expressions and method references.
  • You can chain them using andThen(), compose(), etc.

What is String.chars()?

  • It is a method in the String class (Java 8+).
  • Returns an IntStream of Unicode code points.
  • Each int value represents the character at a position in the string.

Signature:

public IntStream chars()

Why not return Stream<Character>?

  • For performance reasons, `chars()` returns IntStream instead of Stream<Character>.
  • You can easily map the int to char using typecasting.

Example:

String input = "Java";
input.chars().forEach(System.out::println);

Output:

74
97
118
97

Convert to Characters:

input.chars()
     .mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
     .forEach(System.out::println);

Use Case Examples:

  • Count specific characters:
    • long countA = input.chars().filter(ch -> ch == 'a').count();
  • Check if all characters are digits:
    • String str = "12345";
boolean allDigits = str.chars().allMatch(Character::isDigit);
  • Convert to uppercase:
    • String upper = input.chars()
                    .map(Character::toUpperCase)
                    .mapToObj(c -> String.valueOf((char)c))
                    .collect(Collectors.joining());

Note: String.codePoints() is another method which handles Unicode supplementary characters properly.

What is a Substring?

A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters within a string. For a string of length n, there are n*(n+1)/2 possible substrings.

Example:

String input = "abc";
All Substrings = [a, ab, abc, b, bc, c]

Java Code to Print All Substrings:

public class SubstringExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String input = "abc";

        for (int i = 0; i < input.length(); i++) {
            for (int j = i + 1; j <= input.length(); j++) {
                System.out.println(input.substring(i, j));
            }
        }
    }
}

Output:

a
ab
abc
b
bc
c

Time Complexity: O(n²) where n is the length of the string

Store Substrings in a List:

List<String> substrings = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < input.length(); i++) {
    for (int j = i + 1; j <= input.length(); j++) {
        substrings.add(input.substring(i, j));
    }
}
System.out.println(substrings);

What is an Inner Class?

An inner class is a class defined inside another class. You can access its methods or variables by first creating an instance of the outer class, then the inner class.

Example: Non-static Inner Class

public class Outer {
    private String outerField = "Outer Field";

    class Inner {
        void display() {
            System.out.println("Accessing from Inner: " + outerField);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Outer outer = new Outer();
        Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();
        inner.display();
    }
}

Output:

Accessing from Inner: Outer Field

Static Inner Class Example:

public class Outer {
    static class StaticInner {
        void display() {
            System.out.println("Inside Static Inner");
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Outer.StaticInner inner = new Outer.StaticInner();
        inner.display();
    }
}

Output:

Inside Static Inner

Accessing Inner Class Fields:

class Outer {
    class Inner {
        int value = 42;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Outer outer = new Outer();
        Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();
        System.out.println(inner.value);
    }
}

Reflection Access (Advanced):

Outer.Inner innerObj = new Outer().new Inner();
Field field = innerObj.getClass().getDeclaredField("value");
field.setAccessible(true);
System.out.println("Value: " + field.get(innerObj));

🔹 What is ExecutorService?

ExecutorService is an advanced Java concurrency API to manage and control thread execution through a thread pool.

Why use it?

  • Efficient thread reuse
  • Better control of async tasks
  • Lifecycle management of threads

🔹 Ways to Create ExecutorService:

ExecutorService service1 = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
ExecutorService service2 = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);
ExecutorService service3 = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();

🔹 Commonly Used Methods:

  • execute(Runnable task): Executes a Runnable task without expecting a result.
  • <T> submit(Callable<T> task): Submits a task and returns a Future for result.
  • invokeAll(Collection<? extends Callable<T>>): Executes a batch of tasks and waits for all.
  • invokeAny(Collection<? extends Callable<T>>): Executes batch but returns result of the fastest one.
  • shutdown(): Initiates an orderly shutdown after existing tasks complete.
  • shutdownNow(): Attempts to stop all actively executing tasks.
  • isShutdown() / isTerminated(): To check service state.
  • awaitTermination(timeout, unit): Blocks until termination or timeout.

🔹 Example: Using submit()

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3);

Callable<String> task = () -> {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
    return "Task completed";
};

Future<String> future = executor.submit(task);
System.out.println(future.get());

executor.shutdown();

🔹 Example: Using invokeAll()

List<Callable<String>> tasks = List.of(
    () -> "Task1",
    () -> "Task2",
    () -> "Task3"
);

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
List<Future<String>> futures = executor.invokeAll(tasks);

for (Future<String> future : futures) {
    System.out.println(future.get());
}

executor.shutdown();

🔹 Example: Using invokeAny()

String result = executor.invokeAny(List.of(
    () -> {
        Thread.sleep(300);
        return "Fastest";
    },
    () -> {
        Thread.sleep(1000);
        return "Slow";
    }
));
System.out.println("Result: " + result);

🛑 Shutdown vs ShutdownNow:

  • shutdown(): Waits for running tasks to finish
  • shutdownNow(): Interrupts all running tasks immediately

🔹 What is a Marker Interface?

A marker interface is an interface with no methods or fields. It serves as a tag or marker to inform the compiler or JVM that the class implementing this interface has a special behavior.

🔹 Purpose of Marker Interface:

  • Used for **type identification**
  • Gives permission to JVM or frameworks to treat the class in a special way
  • Can be used by frameworks to apply **conditional logic**

🔹 Common Marker Interfaces in Java:

  • java.io.Serializable – Marks a class to be serializable
  • java.lang.Cloneable – Marks a class to support cloning via Object.clone()
  • java.util.EventListener – Marks class as event listener

🔹 Example: Custom Marker Interface

// 1. Create a marker interface
public interface Auditable {}

// 2. Implement in a class
public class User implements Auditable {
    private String name;
    private String email;
}

// 3. Framework logic checking the marker
if (object instanceof Auditable) {
    System.out.println("Audit this entity");
}
