🔹 When to Use Marker Interface?

  • When annotation-based approach isn't suitable (e.g., for legacy systems)
  • To enable conditional processing by a framework or utility
  • To convey metadata without using annotations

✅ Tip: In modern Java (Java 5+), annotations are often preferred over marker interfaces for flexibility and readability.

🔹 What is Spring Cloud?

Spring Cloud provides tools for developers to quickly build distributed systems and microservices using Spring Boot. It handles common patterns such as configuration management, service discovery, circuit breakers, routing, etc.

🔹 Key Components of Spring Cloud

  • 1. Spring Cloud Config – Centralized configuration management
  • 2. Eureka – Service Discovery
  • 3. Spring Cloud Gateway – API Gateway
  • 4. Spring Cloud LoadBalancer – Client-side load balancing
  • 5. Hystrix (Netflix OSS) – Circuit Breaker (now replaced by Resilience4j)
  • 6. Feign – Declarative REST client
  • 7. Zipkin / Sleuth – Distributed Tracing
  • 8. Spring Cloud Bus – Event/message broadcasting

🔹 Spring Cloud Config Example

application.yml (Spring Cloud Config Server)

server:
  port: 8888

spring:
  cloud:
    config:
      server:
        git:
          uri: https://github.com/your-config-repo

Client - bootstrap.yml

spring:
  application:
    name: userservice
  cloud:
    config:
      uri: http://localhost:8888

🔹 Eureka Service Discovery

@EnableEurekaServer // on discovery server
@SpringBootApplication
public class EurekaServerApp {}

@EnableEurekaClient // on microservice
@SpringBootApplication
public class UserServiceApp {}

🔹 Feign Client Example

@FeignClient(name = "orderservice")
public interface OrderClient {
    @GetMapping("/orders/{userId}")
    List<Order> getOrders(@PathVariable Long userId);
}

🔹 Gateway Route Example

spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: user-service
          uri: lb://USER-SERVICE
          predicates:
            - Path=/users/**

🔹 Sleuth + Zipkin Example

spring:
  zipkin:
    base-url: http://localhost:9411
  sleuth:
    sampler:
      probability: 1.0

➡️ Add dependencies: spring-cloud-starter-zipkin and spring-cloud-starter-sleuth

🔹 Resilience4j Circuit Breaker Example

@CircuitBreaker(name = "userService", fallbackMethod = "fallbackMethod")
public String getData() {
    return restTemplate.getForObject("http://SLOW-SERVICE/data", String.class);
}

public String fallbackMethod(Exception e) {
    return "Fallback response";
}

🔹 Spring Cloud Bus

It can propagate config changes across microservices using Kafka or RabbitMQ.

spring:
  cloud:
    bus:
      enabled: true

Endpoint to refresh: POST /actuator/bus-refresh

✅ Summary

  • Spring Cloud helps manage the complexity of distributed systems.
  • Provides out-of-the-box solutions for service discovery, config, gateway, circuit breakers, etc.
  • Most modules integrate easily with Spring Boot using starters.

🔹 Spring Cloud + Microservices = Seamless Distributed Systems

Each Spring Cloud component is designed to solve a common challenge in a microservices-based architecture.

1️⃣ Spring Cloud Config Server

  • 📌 Purpose: Centralized configuration for all microservices
  • 📌 Use Case: Externalize configs in Git/Cloud Storage for all environments (dev, qa, prod)
  • 📌 Benefit: No need to redeploy services on config change (with Spring Cloud Bus)

2️⃣ Eureka Server (Service Discovery)

  • 📌 Purpose: Register and discover microservices dynamically
  • 📌 Use Case: No hardcoded URLs; load-balanced calls using service names
  • 📌 Benefit: Improves scalability and dynamic routing

3️⃣ Spring Cloud Gateway (API Gateway)

  • 📌 Purpose: Entry point for all external traffic to microservices
  • 📌 Use Case: Route requests, apply filters, authentication, throttling
  • 📌 Benefit: Decouple external consumers from internal services

4️⃣ OpenFeign (Declarative REST Client)

  • 📌 Purpose: Simplify REST client communication between services
  • 📌 Use Case: Annotated interfaces calling other microservices
  • 📌 Benefit: Less boilerplate, integrates with Eureka & Ribbon

5️⃣ Spring Cloud LoadBalancer

  • 📌 Purpose: Distribute client requests across multiple service instances
  • 📌 Use Case: RestTemplate, WebClient, Feign clients
  • 📌 Benefit: Helps with fault tolerance and scaling

6️⃣ Spring Cloud Sleuth + Zipkin

  • 📌 Purpose: Distributed tracing between microservices
  • 📌 Use Case: Trace user request flow across multiple services
  • 📌 Benefit: Debugging and latency tracking

7️⃣ Spring Cloud Bus

  • 📌 Purpose: Broadcast config or event changes across services using Kafka/RabbitMQ
  • 📌 Use Case: Refresh config across services on git update
  • 📌 Benefit: Dynamic configuration without service restarts

8️⃣ Spring Cloud Stream

  • 📌 Purpose: Messaging abstraction for asynchronous communication
  • 📌 Use Case: Kafka/RabbitMQ publishers and consumers
  • 📌 Benefit: Event-driven architecture support

9️⃣ Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker (Resilience4j)

  • 📌 Purpose: Prevent failure propagation by cutting off unresponsive services
  • 📌 Use Case: Wrap service calls in fallback logic
  • 📌 Benefit: Increases system resilience

🧩 Summary Table – Spring Cloud to Microservice Mapping

Spring Cloud Component Microservice Concern Solved
Spring Cloud Config Central Configuration
Eureka Service Discovery
Gateway Routing, Security, Throttling
Feign Service-to-Service Calls
LoadBalancer Client-Side Load Balancing
Sleuth & Zipkin Tracing & Monitoring
Bus Broadcast Config Changes
Stream Event-Driven Messaging
Resilience4j Fault Tolerance 


// Java 8 Stream approach to find second highest number
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Optional;

public class SecondHighestFinder {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 50};

        Optional secondHighest = Arrays.stream(numbers)
            .boxed()
            .distinct() // remove duplicates
            .sorted((a, b) -> b - a) // descending order
            .skip(1) // skip the first (highest)
            .findFirst(); // get the second highest

        secondHighest.ifPresentOrElse(
            value -> System.out.println("Second highest number is: " + value),
            () -> System.out.println("No second highest number found")
        );
    }
}
✅ Output:
Second highest number is: 40
🔍 Explanation:
  • .boxed() → Convert int to Integer for stream operations
  • .distinct() → Remove duplicate elements
  • .sorted((a, b) -> b - a) → Sort in descending order
  • .skip(1) → Skip the first (highest) element
  • .findFirst() → Get the second element in sorted stream

🧠 Difference Between Abstraction and Encapsulation:
Aspect Abstraction Encapsulation
Definition Hiding internal details and showing only essential features Wrapping data and methods into a single unit (class)
Goal To focus on what an object does To protect the internal state of the object
Implementation Achieved using abstract classes and interfaces Achieved using access modifiers like private, public, etc.
Use Case Designing systems/interfaces Hiding sensitive data from outside
📦 Encapsulation Example: 

public class Employee {
    private String name; // private field - encapsulated

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public void setName(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}
🔍 Abstraction Example: 

abstract class Animal {
    abstract void makeSound(); // abstract method - only behavior defined
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void makeSound() {
        System.out.println("Bark");
    }
}

🔚 Summary: Abstraction focuses on "what" the object does, while Encapsulation is about "how" to protect the object’s state.

🔍 Key Differences:
Feature Hashtable ConcurrentHashMap
Thread Safety Synchronized on the whole map (less efficient) Thread-safe using segment-level locking (more efficient)
Null Keys/Values Does not allow null key or null value Does not allow null key or null value
Performance Poor under high concurrency Better under high concurrency
Introduced In Legacy, since Java 1.0 Java 1.5 (java.util.concurrent)
📦 Hashtable Example: 

Hashtable<String, String> table = new Hashtable<>();
table.put("A", "Apple");
System.out.println(table.get("A"));
⚙️ ConcurrentHashMap Example: 

ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
map.put("B", "Banana");
System.out.println(map.get("B"));
💡 Tip: Always prefer ConcurrentHashMap for concurrent/multi-threaded applications in modern Java.

✅ What is a Singleton Class?
A singleton class in Java allows only one instance of the class to be created in the entire application.

☕ Basic Singleton Implementation: 

public class Singleton {
  private static Singleton instance;

  private Singleton() {}

  public static Singleton getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {
      instance = new Singleton();
    }
    return instance;
  }
}
⚠️ Ways to Break Singleton:
  • Reflection: Can access private constructor
  • Serialization: Creates a new instance during deserialization
  • Cloning: Can create copy of the object
  • Multithreading: Multiple threads may create multiple instances simultaneously
🛡️ How to Prevent Breaking Singleton:
  • Reflection: Throw exception in constructor if instance already exists
  • Serialization: Implement readResolve()
  • Cloning: Override clone() and throw exception
  • Multithreading: Use synchronized block or double-checked locking
🔒 Double-Checked Locking (Thread Safe Singleton): 

public class Singleton {
  private static volatile Singleton instance;

  private Singleton() {}

  public static Singleton getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {
      synchronized (Singleton.class) {
        if (instance == null) {
          instance = new Singleton();
        }
      }
    }
    return instance;
  }
}
  • Reduces performance overhead using double check
  • volatile ensures visibility and avoids instruction reordering
✔️ Best Practices:
  • Use Enum Singleton for simplest and safest approach
🔐 Enum Singleton: 

public enum Singleton {
  INSTANCE;
}

This is reflection-safe, serialization-safe, and thread-safe by default.

✅ Why Encode Data in REST APIs?
Data encoding ensures safe and secure transmission of information over the network, especially in:
  • URL Parameters
  • Request/Response Bodies
  • Headers
1️⃣ URL Encoding:
  • Use for query parameters and form data
  • Special characters like spaces, &, =, etc. are encoded (e.g., space = %20)

// Example: "name=John Doe&age=25" becomes:
URLEncoder.encode("John Doe", StandardCharsets.UTF_8.toString());
2️⃣ Base64 Encoding:
  • Used to encode binary data (e.g., files, images) or credentials (Basic Auth)
  • Data gets converted to a base64 string

String original = "user:password";
String encoded = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(original.getBytes());
3️⃣ JSON Encoding:
  • JSON itself is a text-based encoding format for structured data
  • Spring Boot automatically serializes objects to JSON using Jackson

// Automatically converted to JSON
@PostMapping("/save")
public ResponseEntity<User> save(@RequestBody User user) {
  return ResponseEntity.ok(userService.save(user));
}
4️⃣ Custom Encoding (Encryption):
  • For sensitive data, encrypt before sending
  • Use AES, RSA, or JWT for secure encoding

// AES Encryption Example
Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES");
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKey);
byte[] encrypted = cipher.doFinal(data.getBytes());
5️⃣ Header Encoding:
  • Custom or authorization headers often use encoded values
  • Example: Basic Auth header

Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNzd29yZA==
🚀 Summary:
  • URLEncoder for URL params
  • Base64 for credentials/files
  • JSON for request/response body
  • Encryption for security-sensitive data

📌 Problem: Generate all permutations of a given string.

✅ Java Code: 

public class Permutations {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String str = "ABC";
        printPermutations(str, "");
    }

    public static void printPermutations(String str, String result) {
        if (str.isEmpty()) {
            System.out.println(result);
            return;
        }

        for (int i = 0; i < str.length(); i++) {
            char ch = str.charAt(i);
            String remaining = str.substring(0, i) + str.substring(i + 1);
            printPermutations(remaining, result + ch);
        }
    }
}
📌 Output for "ABC": 

ABC
ACB
BAC
BCA
CAB
CBA
💡 Note:
  • This solution works for strings with distinct characters.
  • For strings with duplicate characters, use a Set to avoid duplicate permutations.

📌 Problem: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.

✅ Java Code: 

import java.util.HashSet;

public class LongestSubstring {

    public static int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
        int left = 0, right = 0, maxLen = 0;
        HashSet<Character> set = new HashSet<>();

        while (right < s.length()) {
            char ch = s.charAt(right);
            if (!set.contains(ch)) {
                set.add(ch);
                maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, right - left + 1);
                right++;
            } else {
                set.remove(s.charAt(left));
                left++;
            }
        }

        return maxLen;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String input = "abcabcbb";
        System.out.println("Longest length: " + lengthOfLongestSubstring(input));
    }
}
📌 Output: 

Longest length: 3
💡 Explanation:
  • Input: "abcabcbb"
  • The longest substring without repeating characters is "abc", so length = 3
  • This uses the sliding window technique with a HashSet for O(n) performance.

📌 JVM (Java Virtual Machine) Architecture

The JVM is the engine that runs Java bytecode. Its architecture includes the following main components:

🧩 Components of JVM:
  • 1. Class Loader Subsystem: Loads, links, and initializes classes.
  • 2. Method Area: Stores class metadata, static variables, and constants.
  • 3. Heap: Stores objects and instance variables. Shared across threads.
  • 4. Java Stack: Stores frames (method calls) per thread. Each frame has:
    • Local Variables
    • Operand Stack
    • Return Address
  • 5. Program Counter (PC) Register: Holds the address of the currently executing instruction per thread.
  • 6. Native Method Stack: For native (non-Java) method calls like C/C++.
  • 7. Execution Engine: Executes bytecode.
    • Interpreter – Reads bytecode line by line
    • JIT Compiler – Improves performance by compiling repeated bytecode into native code
  • 8. Native Interface: Interface to call native libraries (JNI).
  • 9. Garbage Collector: Automatically deallocates memory used by unreferenced objects.
🧠 JVM Internal Flow:
  1. Java source code (.java) → compiled to bytecode (.class)
  2. Bytecode is loaded by the Class Loader
  3. Stored in Method Area & Heap
  4. Execution Engine runs bytecode using stack, PC, and native stack
  5. Garbage Collector cleans unused objects
📝 Summary:
JVM provides memory management, execution, and runtime environment for Java programs. It abstracts away the platform specifics.

🖼️ Want Diagram? I can generate a JVM architecture diagram if you'd like. Just say the word! 😊

🧱 LinkedList Node Class:
```java class Node { int data; Node next; Node(int data) { this.data = data; this.next = null; } } ```
🔁 Custom LinkedList:
```java class MyLinkedList { Node head; public void add(int data) { Node newNode = new Node(data); if (head == null) { head = newNode; } else { Node current = head; while (current.next != null) { current = current.next; } current.next = newNode; } } public void printList() { Node current = head; while (current != null) { System.out.print(current.data + " "); current = current.next; } System.out.println(); } } ```
📚 Custom Stack (LIFO):
```java class MyStack { Node top; public void push(int data) { Node newNode = new Node(data); newNode.next = top; top = newNode; } public int pop() { if (top == null) throw new RuntimeException("Stack is empty!"); int val = top.data; top = top.next; return val; } public boolean isEmpty() { return top == null; } } ```
🚦 Custom Queue (FIFO):
```java class MyQueue { Node front, rear; public void enqueue(int data) { Node newNode = new Node(data); if (rear == null) { front = rear = newNode; } else { rear.next = newNode; rear = newNode; } } public int dequeue() { if (front == null) throw new RuntimeException("Queue is empty!"); int val = front.data; front = front.next; if (front == null) rear = null; return val; } public boolean isEmpty() { return front == null; } } ```
🧪 Usage Example:
```java public class TestCustomDS { public static void main(String[] args) { // LinkedList MyLinkedList list = new MyLinkedList(); list.add(1); list.add(2); list.add(3); list.printList(); // 1 2 3 // Stack MyStack stack = new MyStack(); stack.push(10); stack.push(20); System.out.println(stack.pop()); // 20 // Queue MyQueue queue = new MyQueue(); queue.enqueue(100); queue.enqueue(200); System.out.println(queue.dequeue()); // 100 } } ``` 📌 Summary:
  • 📚 Stack uses LIFO — push at top, pop from top
  • 🚦 Queue uses FIFO — enqueue at rear, dequeue from front
  • 🔗 LinkedList stores data dynamically using node pointers

💡 Reason:
Java's Garbage Collector (GC) automatically reclaims memory of unreferenced objects. However, **OutOfMemoryError** can still occur due to reasons like:

🚨 Common Causes:
  • 1. Memory Leak: Unused objects are still referenced, preventing GC from reclaiming them.
  • 2. Large Data Structures: Storing large collections (like lists, maps) in memory without limit.
  • 3. Infinite Object Creation: In loops or recursive calls without base case.
  • 4. Incorrect JVM Heap Settings: Heap size is too small to hold all objects.
  • 5. Improper Cleanup: Holding on to references like static fields, thread-locals, caches etc.
  • 6. Permanent Generation / Metaspace Overflow: Too many loaded classes or large method metadata (especially in older Java versions).

📍 Example: ```java List memoryHog = new ArrayList<>(); while (true) { memoryHog.add(new byte[1024 * 1024]); // 1 MB } ```
💥 Output: ``` Exception in thread "main" java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space ```
🛠️ Solutions:
  • ✅ Fix memory leaks by reviewing references.
  • ✅ Use proper data structures (bounded queues, weak references).
  • ✅ Increase heap size using JVM options: -Xmx1024m, -Xms512m
  • ✅ Use memory profiling tools like VisualVM, JProfiler.
🔍 Summary:
  • Garbage Collection reclaims only unreferenced memory.
  • If objects are still referenced or memory grows uncontrollably — GC cannot help.
  • Hence, memory leaks or huge object graphs lead to OutOfMemoryError.

Java 8 introduced powerful enhancements in the Collections framework:

  • 1. forEach()
    - Allows easy iteration over elements using lambda.
    list.forEach(System.out::println);

  • 2. removeIf()
    - Removes elements that satisfy a predicate.
    list.removeIf(s -> s.length() > 5);

  • 3. replaceAll()
    - Replaces each element using a unary operator.
    list.replaceAll(String::toUpperCase);

  • 4. sort(Comparator)
    - Allows lambda-based sorting directly on List.
    list.sort((a, b) -> a.compareTo(b));

  • 5. Map's new methods:
    • forEach(BiConsumer)
    • getOrDefault()
    • putIfAbsent()
    • merge()
    • compute(), computeIfAbsent(), computeIfPresent()
    • replaceAll()

  • 6. Stream API
    - Not part of Collections per se but enables powerful operations on collections.
    list.stream().filter(s -> s.startsWith("A")).collect(Collectors.toList());

  • 7. Default and Static methods in interfaces:
    - Java 8 added ability to add default implementation inside interfaces like Collection, List, Map, etc.

  • 8. Spliterator
    - For parallel traversal and processing.
    Spliterator spliterator = list.spliterator();
📝 Summary:
  • Java 8 made collections more expressive and concise using functional programming.
  • Stream API and enhanced collection methods reduced boilerplate significantly.
  • Maps became much more powerful with conditional operations.

💡 Java 8 focuses more on functional-style exception handling:

  • 1. Exception Handling in Lambda Expressions
    - Lambda expressions can throw exceptions, but they must be unchecked or explicitly handled.
    list.forEach(item -> { try { if(item == null) throw new RuntimeException("Null found"); } catch(Exception e) { e.printStackTrace(); } });

  • 2. Functional Interfaces don’t support checked exceptions directly
    - You need to wrap them manually or use a custom wrapper.
    interface CheckedFunction { R apply(T t) throws Exception; }

  • 3. Optional - Null-Safe Handling
    - Use Optional to avoid NullPointerException.
    Optional value = Optional.ofNullable(getValue());
    value.orElse("default");

  • 4. Stream API Exception Wrapping
    - When using streams, exceptions must be handled inside lambdas.
    list.stream().map(item -> {
      try {
        return riskyCall(item);
      } catch (Exception e) {
        return "default";
      }
    }).collect(Collectors.toList());

  • 5. Custom Wrappers for Checked Exceptions in Functional Context
    - Example for rethrowing a checked exception:
    static <T, R> Function<T, R> wrap(CheckedFunction<T, R> func) { return i -> { try { return func.apply(i); } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } }; }
✅ Summary:
  • Java 8 encourages safe programming using Optional instead of null checks.
  • Lambda expressions require creative handling of checked exceptions.
  • Custom wrappers help manage checked exceptions in streams and functional interfaces.

💡 Use an abstract class when:
  • 1. You want to share common code:
    Abstract class allows you to define methods with a default implementation.
    abstract class Animal {
    void breathe() { System.out.println("Breathing..."); }
    abstract void sound();
    }

  • 2. You need to declare non-static/non-final fields:
    Abstract classes can have instance variables to maintain state.

  • 3. You want to control inheritance:
    Abstract classes support constructors and can enforce inheritance structure better.

  • 4. You require version compatibility:
    Adding new methods in an abstract class with default behavior is safer than changing interfaces (unless using Java 8+ default methods).

  • 5. You want to provide template methods:
    Abstract classes support the Template Method Pattern where a base class defines a skeleton of an operation.
🚫 Avoid Abstract Class when:
  • You only need method signatures (use interface instead).
  • You want multiple inheritance (Java allows multiple interfaces, but not multiple classes).
✅ Summary:
  • Use Abstract Class: When you have common behavior and state to share.
  • Use Interface: When you only define capabilities/behavior contracts.

💥 What is Deadlock?
Deadlock is a situation where two or more threads are blocked forever, each waiting on the other to release a lock.

🧵 Example of Deadlock: 

class A {
  synchronized void methodA(B b) {
    System.out.println("Thread 1: Holding A and waiting for B");
    b.last();
  }

  synchronized void last() {
    System.out.println("Inside A.last()");
  }
}

class B {
  synchronized void methodB(A a) {
    System.out.println("Thread 2: Holding B and waiting for A");
    a.last();
  }

  synchronized void last() {
    System.out.println("Inside B.last()");
  }
}
⚠️ Problem: If Thread 1 holds lock on A and waits for B, and Thread 2 holds lock on B and waits for A → deadlock!

✅ How to Avoid Deadlock:
  • 1. Lock ordering: Always acquire locks in a consistent global order across all threads.
  • 2. Use tryLock(): Use ReentrantLock.tryLock() to avoid waiting indefinitely.
  • 3. Timeout: Set a timeout to prevent infinite waiting on a lock.
  • 4. Avoid nested locks: Try to acquire only one lock at a time whenever possible.
  • 5. Detect deadlocks: Use Java tools like jconsole or VisualVM to detect deadlock threads.
🔐 Example using tryLock to prevent deadlock: 

ReentrantLock lock1 = new ReentrantLock();
ReentrantLock lock2 = new ReentrantLock();

if (lock1.tryLock(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
  if (lock2.tryLock(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    try {
      // do work
    } finally {
      lock2.unlock();
      lock1.unlock();
    }
  }
}

📌 Definition:
A hashing collision occurs when two different objects produce the same hash code, and thus they are mapped to the same bucket in a hash-based data structure like HashMap or HashSet.

📦 Example: 

class CustomKey {
  int id;

  CustomKey(int id) {
    this.id = id;
  }

  @Override
  public int hashCode() {
    return 1; // Same hash for every object
  }

  @Override
  public boolean equals(Object obj) {
    return this.id == ((CustomKey)obj).id;
  }
}
If you insert multiple CustomKey objects into a HashMap, they’ll all go into the same bucket → Collision.

🧠 Why It's a Problem:
  • Reduces performance to O(n) from O(1) for lookup/insert.
  • Increased risk of DOS attacks via hash flooding (intentionally causing collisions).
🛡️ How Java Handles It (HashMap):
  • Initially uses a linked list to handle collisions in the same bucket.
  • If the number of entries in a bucket exceeds a threshold (usually 8), it converts to a balanced tree (red-black tree) to improve performance.
✅ Best Practices to Avoid Collisions:
  • Override both hashCode() and equals() properly.
  • Use prime numbers and good distribution logic in hashCode() implementation.
  • Keep hash-based collections like HashMap, HashSet properly sized.

👨‍🏫 What is a SQL JOIN?
A SQL JOIN is used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them.

🧱 Sample Tables: 

Table: Employees
+----+--------+------------+
| ID | Name   | Dept_ID    |
+----+--------+------------+
| 1  | Alice  | 101        |
| 2  | Bob    | 102        |
| 3  | Carol  | 103        |
| 4  | David  | null       |
+----+--------+------------+

Table: Departments
+---------+--------------+
| Dept_ID | Dept_Name    |
+---------+--------------+
| 101     | HR           |
| 102     | IT           |
| 104     | Finance      |
+---------+--------------+
1️⃣ INNER JOIN
Returns records that have matching values in both tables. 

SELECT e.Name, d.Dept_Name
FROM Employees e
INNER JOIN Departments d
ON e.Dept_ID = d.Dept_ID;
✅ Output: Only employees with a matching department.
2️⃣ LEFT JOIN (or LEFT OUTER JOIN)
Returns all records from the left table and matched records from the right table. 

SELECT e.Name, d.Dept_Name
FROM Employees e
LEFT JOIN Departments d
ON e.Dept_ID = d.Dept_ID;
✅ Output: All employees. If no match, Dept_Name is NULL.
3️⃣ RIGHT JOIN (or RIGHT OUTER JOIN)
Returns all records from the right table and the matched records from the left table. 

SELECT e.Name, d.Dept_Name
FROM Employees e
RIGHT JOIN Departments d
ON e.Dept_ID = d.Dept_ID;
✅ Output: All departments. If no match, Name is NULL.
4️⃣ FULL JOIN (or FULL OUTER JOIN)
Returns all records when there is a match in either table. 

SELECT e.Name, d.Dept_Name
FROM Employees e
FULL OUTER JOIN Departments d
ON e.Dept_ID = d.Dept_ID;
✅ Output: All employees and departments with or without a match.
5️⃣ CROSS JOIN
Returns the Cartesian product of both tables (every row from one joined with every row of the other). 

SELECT e.Name, d.Dept_Name
FROM Employees e
CROSS JOIN Departments d;
✅ Output: All combinations of employees and departments.
6️⃣ SELF JOIN
A self join is a regular join but the table is joined with itself. 

SELECT A.Name AS Employee1, B.Name AS Employee2
FROM Employees A, Employees B
WHERE A.Dept_ID = B.Dept_ID AND A.ID <> B.ID;
✅ Output: Employees in the same department.

💡 What is Indexing?
An Index in SQL is a performance optimization feature that allows the database to find and access data quickly, just like an index in a book.

⚡ Why Use Indexing?
  • 🔍 Faster SELECT queries
  • 📦 Efficient searching & filtering
  • 🧭 Helps on large datasets and WHERE conditions
  • 📊 Improves performance of JOINs, ORDER BY, GROUP BY
🧪 Example:
Suppose you have a large Employees table with 10 million rows. 

CREATE TABLE Employees (
  ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(100),
  Email VARCHAR(100),
  Salary DECIMAL(10,2)
);
Searching by email without index: 

SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Email = 'user@example.com';
-- ⏳ Slow full table scan
Now, add an index: 

CREATE INDEX idx_email ON Employees(Email);
After indexing: 

SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Email = 'user@example.com';
-- ⚡ Faster! Uses binary search on index
🛑 When NOT to Use Indexing?
  • Too many indexes = slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
  • On small tables – overhead isn't worth it
  • On columns with low selectivity (e.g. gender, status)
📚 Types of Indexes:
  • PRIMARY Index – Automatically created on primary key
  • UNIQUE Index – Ensures all values are unique
  • COMPOSITE Index – On multiple columns
  • FULLTEXT Index – For text search (MySQL)
  • SPATIAL Index – For geo-data
🧠 Summary:
  • ✅ Index improves read/query performance
  • ⚠️ Can slow down writes (insert/update/delete)
  • 🎯 Use on frequently searched or joined columns

🧠 Requirement:
Find the 4th highest salary from the Employees table.

✅ Query using DISTINCT and LIMIT / OFFSET (MySQL): 

SELECT DISTINCT Salary
FROM Employees
ORDER BY Salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 3;
-- This returns the 4th highest salary (0-indexed)
✅ Query using Subquery (Works in most DBs like Oracle, PostgreSQL): 

SELECT MIN(Salary) AS FourthHighestSalary
FROM (
  SELECT DISTINCT Salary
  FROM Employees
  ORDER BY Salary DESC
  LIMIT 4
) AS TopFour;
✅ Query using ROW_NUMBER() (PostgreSQL, SQL Server, etc): 

SELECT Salary
FROM (
  SELECT Salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS rn
  FROM Employees
) AS RankedSalaries
WHERE rn = 4;
📌 Note: If salaries are not unique and you want the 4th **distinct** salary, use DENSE_RANK() instead of ROW_NUMBER().

No, Java does not allow safe forceful termination of threads.

  • 🛑 Thread.stop() is deprecated due to unsafe behavior.
  • ✅ Use Thread.interrupt() and cooperative checks inside your thread logic.
  • ✅ Use Future.cancel(true) for interruptible tasks via ExecutorService.
  • 🧠 Design tasks to check for interruption and exit cleanly.

while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
   // safe logic
}

📌 What is Inheritance?
Inheritance is a mechanism in Java where one class inherits the properties (fields and methods) of another class.

✅ Benefits:
  • Code reusability
  • Method overriding (polymorphism)
  • Better maintainability
🔰 Syntax: 
class Parent { }
class Child extends Parent { }
🧩 Types of Inheritance in Java:
  • Single Inheritance ✅
  • Multilevel Inheritance ✅
  • Hierarchical Inheritance ✅
  • Multiple Inheritance ❌ (Not supported with classes, only with interfaces)
🤔 What if Parent throws Exception?
  • If the parent method throws a checked exception, the child must either declare it or handle it.
  • If the parent method throws an unchecked exception (like NullPointerException), the child doesn't need to declare or handle it explicitly.
✅ Example: 
class Parent {
    void show() throws Exception {
        System.out.println("Parent show");
        throw new Exception("Checked Exception");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void show() throws Exception { // Must declare or handle
        System.out.println("Child show");
        super.show();
    }
}
✅ Example with Unchecked Exception: 
class Parent {
    void display() {
        throw new NullPointerException("NPE");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Child display");
        super.display(); // No need to handle
    }
}
⚠️ Summary:
  • Checked exceptions must be declared or handled in child if overridden.
  • Unchecked exceptions don’t need to be declared or handled in child.

🚫 No, you cannot start a thread twice in Java.

Once a thread has been started and completed execution, calling start() again on the same thread instance will throw a java.lang.IllegalThreadStateException.

✅ Example: 
public class MyThread extends Thread {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Running thread...");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MyThread t1 = new MyThread();
        t1.start(); // ✅ First time, will work

        t1.start(); // ❌ Second time, throws exception
    }
}
🛑 Output: 
Running thread...
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalThreadStateException
      at java.lang.Thread.start(Thread.java:708)
⚠️ Why?
  • Each thread object can be started only once.
  • If you need to run it again, create a new Thread instance.
✅ Correct Way: 
MyThread t1 = new MyThread();
t1.start();

MyThread t2 = new MyThread(); // New instance
t2.start();

🔄 What is Synchronization?
Synchronization is a way to control access to shared resources by multiple threads to avoid data inconsistency or race conditions.
🧩 1. Synchronized Instance Method
This locks the current object (`this`) so that only one thread can access any synchronized method at a time on the same object. 
public class Counter {
    private int count = 0;

    public synchronized void increment() {
        count++;
    }
}
✅ All synchronized methods share the same lock on the current object.
🔒 2. Synchronized Block
Use this when you only want a specific portion of the code to be synchronized rather than the whole method. 
public void increment() {
    synchronized(this) {
        count++;
    }
}
✅ More efficient than synchronizing the whole method.
🧊 3. Static Synchronized Method
This locks the class object (`ClassName.class`) instead of the current object. 
public class Counter {
    private static int count = 0;

    public static synchronized void increment() {
        count++;
    }
}
✅ Useful when working with static data.
🧱 4. Synchronization on Custom Object
You can lock on any object. 
private final Object lock = new Object();

public void increment() {
    synchronized(lock) {
        count++;
    }
}
✅ Helps in fine-grained locking.
⚠️ Caveats & Notes:
  • Synchronization adds overhead.
  • Don't synchronize on objects that can be externally accessed (like `String`, as they are interned).
  • Can cause deadlocks if not designed carefully.
🧪 Example Use Case: 
public class MyThread extends Thread {
    Counter counter;

    MyThread(Counter c) {
        this.counter = c;
    }

    public void run() {
        for(int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
            counter.increment();
        }
    }
}

public class Counter {
    private int count = 0;

    public synchronized void increment() {
        count++;
    }

    public int getCount() {
        return count;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Counter c = new Counter();
        MyThread t1 = new MyThread(c);
        MyThread t2 = new MyThread(c);
        t1.start();
        t2.start();
        t1.join();
        t2.join();
        System.out.println("Count: " + c.getCount());
    }
}
🧾 Without synchronization, the result may be less than 2000 due to race condition.

Java threads can exist in one of the following states defined by the `Thread.State` enum:
1️⃣ NEW
When a thread object is created but not yet started. 
Thread t = new Thread();  // State is NEW
2️⃣ RUNNABLE
The thread is ready to run and waiting for CPU time. It may be running or waiting in the thread scheduler. 
t.start();  // Now in RUNNABLE state
3️⃣ BLOCKED
The thread is waiting to acquire a lock (monitor) that another thread holds. 
synchronized(lock) {
    // Thread 1 has acquired lock
    // Thread 2 trying to enter same block is BLOCKED
}
4️⃣ WAITING
The thread is waiting indefinitely for another thread to perform a particular action (like notify). 
synchronized(lock) {
    lock.wait();  // Thread enters WAITING state
}
5️⃣ TIMED_WAITING
Waiting for a specific amount of time (sleep, join with timeout, wait with timeout). 
Thread.sleep(1000);  // TIMED_WAITING
thread.join(500);    // TIMED_WAITING
lock.wait(2000);     // TIMED_WAITING
6️⃣ TERMINATED
The thread has completed execution or has been aborted due to an exception. 
public void run() {
    System.out.println("Done");
}
// After run completes → TERMINATED
🧪 Check Thread State 
Thread t = new Thread(() -> {});
System.out.println(t.getState()); // NEW
t.start();
System.out.println(t.getState()); // RUNNABLE or others
📌 Summary Table:
State Description
NEW Thread created, not yet started
RUNNABLE Ready to run or running
BLOCKED Waiting for monitor lock
WAITING Waiting indefinitely
TIMED_WAITING Waiting with timeout
TERMINATED Finished execution

✅ Yes, we can create a constructor as private in Java.
📌 What Happens If Constructor is Private?
  • It **restricts object creation** from outside the class.
  • Used in **Singleton**, **Factory Pattern**, and **Utility classes** (like `java.lang.Math` or `Collections`).
  • You can’t do: MyClass obj = new MyClass(); from outside the class.
✅ Example: Singleton Pattern Using Private Constructor 
public class MySingleton {
  private static MySingleton instance;

  private MySingleton() {
    // private constructor
  }

  public static MySingleton getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {
      instance = new MySingleton();
    }
    return instance;
  }
}
🔒 Attempting to create object outside will fail: 
MySingleton obj = new MySingleton();  // ❌ Compile-time error
🛠 Use Cases of Private Constructors:
  • Singleton Design Pattern
  • Utility/helper classes
  • Static factory methods
  • Prevent instantiation of abstract base classes or constants-only classes

📌 In Java, the catch blocks are executed from top to bottom, and the first block that matches the thrown exception type will handle it.
✅ Correct Order:
  • Catch blocks should go from most specific to most general.
  • If a more general exception (like Exception) comes before a specific one (like ArithmeticException), it will cause a compile-time error.
🔍 Example: 
try {
    int x = 10 / 0;
} catch (ArithmeticException e) {
    System.out.println("Caught ArithmeticException");
} catch (Exception e) {
    System.out.println("Caught general Exception");
}
✅ Output: Caught ArithmeticException
❌ Wrong Order Example (Causes Compile Error): 
try {
    int x = 10 / 0;
} catch (Exception e) {
    System.out.println("General Exception");
} catch (ArithmeticException e) { // ❌ Unreachable
    System.out.println("Specific ArithmeticException");
}
💡 Why? The general Exception block will catch everything, so specific blocks after it are unreachable.
✅ Rule to Remember: Catch blocks must go from:
  • IOException → RuntimeException → Exception → Throwable

Java provides a hierarchy of exception classes to handle various kinds of errors.

🔽 Here's a simple diagram representation: 

                      ┌────────────┐
                      │ Throwable  │
                      └────┬───────┘
               ┌───────────┴─────────────┐
         ┌─────▼─────┐            ┌──────▼──────┐
         │  Error    │            │ Exception   │
         └───────────┘            └──────┬──────┘
                                   ┌─────▼────────────┐
                            ┌──────┤ RuntimeException │
                            │      └──────┬───────────┘
                            │     ┌───────▼────────┐
                            │     │ NullPointer... │
                            │     │ ArrayIndex...  │
                            │     │ IllegalArg...  │
                            │     └────────────────┘
                            │
                            └── Checked Exceptions:
                                  ┌──────────────┐
                                  │ IOException  │
                                  │ SQLException │
                                  └──────────────┘
🔍 Top Level: Throwable
  • The superclass of all errors and exceptions.
➡️ Error: Represents serious problems that a reasonable application should not try to catch.
  • OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, etc.
➡️ Exception: Conditions that a program might want to catch.
  • Checked: Must be declared or handled (e.g., IOException, SQLException).
  • Unchecked (Runtime): Not required to handle (e.g., NullPointerException, ArithmeticException).
✅ Summary:
  • Error – for JVM errors (e.g., memory issues)
  • Checked Exception – must handle explicitly
  • Unchecked Exception – runtime issues like logic errors

🔹 What are Generics?
Generics enable types (classes and interfaces) to be parameters when defining classes, interfaces and methods. They allow for type-safe data structures.
✅ Why Generics?
  • Compile-time type checking
  • Avoids type casting
  • Code reusability
🔧 Example 1: Generic Class 

public class Box<T> {
    private T item;

    public void set(T item) {
        this.item = item;
    }

    public T get() {
        return item;
    }
}

Box<String> stringBox = new Box<>();
stringBox.set("Hello");
System.out.println(stringBox.get());  // Output: Hello
🔁 Example 2: Generic Method 

public class GenericMethodExample {
    public static <T> void printArray(T[] array) {
        for (T item : array) {
            System.out.println(item);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Integer[] intArray = {1, 2, 3};
        String[] strArray = {"A", "B", "C"};
        printArray(intArray);
        printArray(strArray);
    }
}
🧠 Bounded Types: 

public class NumberBox<T extends Number> {
    private T num;

    public void set(T num) {
        this.num = num;
    }

    public T get() {
        return num;
    }
}
🔹 This restricts T to subclasses of `Number`.
♻️ Wildcards:
  • ? – unknown type
  • ? extends T – upper bound
  • ? super T – lower bound

// List of unknown type
public void printList(List<?> list) {
    for (Object obj : list) {
        System.out.println(obj);
    }
}
📌 Summary:
  • Use Generics to enforce compile-time safety
  • Reusability and abstraction
  • Wildcard types offer flexibility

🧑‍💻 Step 1: Create a class 

class Person {
    String firstName;
    String lastName;

    public Person(String firstName, String lastName) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
    }

    public String getFirstName() { return firstName; }
    public String getLastName() { return lastName; }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return firstName + " " + lastName;
    }
}
🔁 Step 2: Sort using Comparator (Java 8) 

List<Person> people = Arrays.asList(
    new Person("John", "Doe"),
    new Person("Alice", "Smith"),
    new Person("John", "Adams"),
    new Person("Alice", "Brown")
);

people.sort(Comparator
    .comparing(Person::getFirstName)
    .thenComparing(Person::getLastName)
);

people.forEach(System.out::println);
📦 Output: 

Alice Brown
Alice Smith
John Adams
John Doe
✅ Summary:
  • Use Comparator.comparing() for clean, functional-style sorting.
  • thenComparing() allows secondary sorting criteria.
  • This approach is null-safe if used with Comparator.nullsFirst() or nullsLast().

🔍 Definition:

try-with-resources is a feature introduced in Java 7 that automatically closes resources like InputStream, BufferedReader, FileWriter, etc., after the try block, even if an exception occurs.

🧑‍💻 Syntax Example: 

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.FileReader;
import java.io.IOException;

public class TryWithResourcesExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("file.txt"))) {
            String line = reader.readLine();
            System.out.println(line);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            e.printStackTrace();
        }
    }
}
📘 Notes:
  • Any object used in try-with-resources must implement AutoCloseable (or Closeable).
  • Closes resources automatically at the end of try block.
  • Reduces boilerplate code (no need for finally block).
✅ Advantages:
  • Clean and concise code.
  • Prevents resource leaks.
  • Supports multiple resources in one try block.
📦 Java 9 Enhancement:

From Java 9 onward, you can use variables declared outside of try in the try-with-resources block if they are effectively final. 


BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("file.txt"));
try (reader) {
    // works in Java 9+
}
      


class MyThread extends Thread {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Thread running via Thread class");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MyThread t = new MyThread();
        t.start();
    }
}
      


class MyRunnable implements Runnable {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Thread running via Runnable");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread t = new Thread(new MyRunnable());
        t.start();
    }
}
      


public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("Thread via Lambda"));
        t.start();
    }
}
      


import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ExecutorService service = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
        service.execute(() -> System.out.println("Thread via ExecutorService"));
        service.shutdown();
    }
}
      


import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService service = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
        Callable task = () -> "Callable Result";
        Future<String> future = service.submit(task);
        System.out.println(future.get());
        service.shutdown();
    }
}

Used to submit a task and get a Future object.
- Accepts both Runnable and Callable.
- Returns a Future which can be used to get the result or check task completion.
- Useful for tasks that return a value or may throw exceptions.

Example: 

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1);
Future<String> future = executor.submit(() -> {
    return "Hello from submit!";
});
System.out.println(future.get()); // prints: Hello from submit!
executor.shutdown();

Used to execute a task without expecting a result.
- Accepts only Runnable.
- Doesn’t return any value (no Future).
- Suitable for fire-and-forget type tasks.

Example: 

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1);
executor.execute(() -> System.out.println("Hello from execute!"));
executor.shutdown();

Aspect submit() execute()
Return Type Future void
Supports Callable ✅ ❌
Exception Handling Captured in Future Throws at runtime
Use Case Need result Just run the task

This is the core pattern used.
- A pool of worker threads is created.
- Tasks are submitted and assigned to threads from the pool.
- Prevents the overhead of creating a new thread per task.
- Enhances performance and resource management.

Real usage: Executors.newFixedThreadPool()

Used for task execution policies.
- Different implementations of Executor provide different strategies.
- For example: CachedThreadPool, FixedThreadPool, SingleThreadExecutor.
- Each strategy controls how threads are allocated and reused.

Every task is treated as a command object.
- Implemented using Runnable or Callable.
- Encapsulates all information needed to perform an action (task).
- Executor executes the command independently.

Used internally to decouple task submission and execution.
- Tasks (producers) are submitted to a queue.
- Worker threads (consumers) take tasks from the queue and execute them.
- Improves throughput and responsiveness.

No, fields don't have to be final, but it's highly recommended. Using final gives compile-time safety and ensures the field is not reassigned.

- Internal code might reassign the field by mistake.
- Doesn't guarantee immutability at compile time.
- Less clarity and safety in multi-threaded environments.

- Declare class as final.
- Declare all fields as private final.
- Initialize them in the constructor only.
- Don’t expose setters.
- Return defensive copies for mutable fields.

substring() is used to extract a portion of a string. It takes beginIndex and endIndex and returns the characters in that range.

Internally, it creates a new char[] that contains only the substring characters. It does not share the original array like it used to in Java 7.

- Java 7: Shares char[] → risk of memory leak
- Java 8: Copies to new char[] → safe and clean
- Preferred for modern apps and memory-safe logic. 

String str1 = "abc";
- Stored in **String Constant Pool** (inside Heap).
- If another `"abc"` literal exists, it will be **reused**.
- Memory efficient. 

String str2 = new String("abc");
- Always creates a **new object** in the Heap.
- Even if "abc" exists in the string pool.
- Not memory efficient. 


String str1 = "abc";
String str2 = new String("abc");

System.out.println(str1 == str2);      // false (different objects)
System.out.println(str1.equals(str2)); // true (same value)
- == compares object **references**
- equals() compares **values**

Use intern() method:

String str3 = new String("abc").intern();
System.out.println(str1 == str3); // true
- `intern()` checks if literal is in pool → returns reference. 


@Test
void testExceptionThrown() {
    IllegalArgumentException ex = assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> {
        myService.validateInput(null);
    });
    assertEquals("Input cannot be null", ex.getMessage());
}
- ✅ Checks both **type** and **message** of the exception 


import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

@Test
void testUsingAssertJ() {
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> myService.validateInput(null))
        .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)
        .hasMessage("Input cannot be null");
}
- ✅ Clean, readable and **chained assertion** style

void testControllerException() throws Exception {
    mockMvc.perform(get("/api/test/exception"))
           .andExpect(status().isBadRequest())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.message").value("Invalid input"));
}
- ✅ Use this to test **@ControllerAdvice**, exception handlers, etc.

A bean is simply a Java object managed by Spring. Beans represent the core building blocks of a Spring application.

Example: 

@Component
public class MyService {
    // business logic
}

The ApplicationContext is the heart of the Spring IoC container. It is responsible for instantiating, configuring, and managing beans.

Example: 

ApplicationContext context = 
    new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);
MyService service = context.getBean(MyService.class);

DI is the process where Spring injects dependencies into a class (like service into controller) instead of the class creating them itself.

Example: 

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    @Autowired
    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}
Spring provides the PaymentService at runtime 🎯

  1. 1. Bean
    A Bean is an object managed by the Spring container. These are the building blocks of your application, defined with annotations like @Component, @Service, @Repository, or in XML config.
  2. 2. ApplicationContext
    It's the heart of Spring IOC. It creates, wires, configures, and manages the lifecycle of beans. It also provides features like internationalization, event propagation, and resource loading.
  3. 3. BeanFactory
    It's the root interface for accessing the Spring container. It lazily loads beans.
    ApplicationContext is a superset of BeanFactory and is generally preferred.
  4. 4. Dependency Injection (DI)
    Core of IOC. The control of object creation and injection is handed over to the Spring container.
    Two types: Constructor Injection and Setter Injection.
  5. 5. Configuration Metadata
    Defines how beans are configured: XML, Java-based config (using @Configuration), or annotations.
  6. 6. Bean Definition
    Contains metadata like class name, scope, lifecycle callbacks, and dependencies for a bean, used internally by Spring.
  7. 7. BeanPostProcessor
    Interface used to intercept bean creation to modify or wrap bean instances, e.g., for proxying or custom logic.
  8. 8. BeanFactoryPostProcessor
    Similar to BeanPostProcessor, but it allows modifying the Bean definitions before the beans are instantiated.
  9. 9. IoC Container
    The container (like ApplicationContext) that manages the entire lifecycle of beans and handles the inversion of control.
👉 TL;DR: Spring IOC is a powerful mechanism where the container handles object creation and dependency management, letting developers focus on business logic.

  • 1. Isolation: Each microservice runs in its own container, with its own environment, dependencies, and libraries — avoiding conflicts.
  • 2. Portability: Containers include everything the service needs, making it easy to run the same microservice across dev, QA, staging, and prod environments.
  • 3. Scalability: Containers are lightweight and fast to start, so microservices can scale in and out easily based on traffic.
  • 4. Resource Efficiency: Containers use fewer resources than virtual machines and allow better utilization of server capacity.
  • 5. DevOps Friendly: Works great with CI/CD pipelines, Docker, Kubernetes — supporting rapid development, testing, and deployment cycles.
  • 6. Rollback & Versioning: Containers can be versioned and rolled back easily using image tags.
  • 7. Easy Monitoring & Logging: Tools like Prometheus, Grafana, and ELK work seamlessly with containerized microservices for better observability.
  • 8. Faster Recovery: In case of failure, containers can be restarted or replaced quickly using orchestration tools like Kubernetes.

In short: Containers give microservices agility, efficiency, and independence — exactly what you need to run them in a distributed environment like the cloud.

  • 100 Continue: The server has received the request headers, and the client should proceed to send the request body.
  • 101 Switching Protocols: The requester has asked the server to switch protocols.

  • 200 OK: The request succeeded.
  • 201 Created: The request succeeded and a resource was created.
  • 202 Accepted: The request has been accepted for processing, but the processing is not completed.
  • 204 No Content: The server successfully processed the request, but is not returning any content.

  • 301 Moved Permanently: The URL of the requested resource has been changed permanently.
  • 302 Found: The resource resides temporarily under a different URI.
  • 304 Not Modified: The resource has not been modified since the last request.

  • 400 Bad Request: The server could not understand the request due to invalid syntax.
  • 401 Unauthorized: The client must authenticate itself to get the requested response.
  • 403 Forbidden: The client does not have access rights to the content.
  • 404 Not Found: The server cannot find the requested resource.
  • 405 Method Not Allowed: The method is not allowed for the requested URL.
  • 409 Conflict: The request conflicts with the current state of the server.
  • 429 Too Many Requests: The user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time.

  • 500 Internal Server Error: The server encountered an unexpected condition.
  • 501 Not Implemented: The server does not support the functionality required to fulfill the request.
  • 502 Bad Gateway: The server, while acting as a gateway or proxy, received an invalid response.
  • 503 Service Unavailable: The server is not ready to handle the request (e.g. maintenance or overload).
  • 504 Gateway Timeout: The server did not receive a timely response from an upstream server.

Explanation:
Java does not recommend forcefully stopping threads (like using Thread.stop()). Instead, we use interrupt() to request a thread to stop, and the thread should handle that request cooperatively.

Code Example: 

class MyTask implements Runnable {
    public void run() {
        while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
            System.out.println("Running...");
            try {
                Thread.sleep(1000);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                System.out.println("Thread was interrupted during sleep");
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // Re-set the interrupt flag
                break;
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Thread exiting...");
    }
}

Thread t = new Thread(new MyTask());
t.start();

// Sleep main for 3 seconds then interrupt
Thread.sleep(3000);
t.interrupt();

Three ways to check interruption:
  • Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() → Checks and does not clear the flag
  • Thread.interrupted() → Checks and clears the interrupt status
  • Catch InterruptedException if blocking methods are used

if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
    System.out.println("Thread was interrupted");
}

📌 Checked Exceptions
  • Inherit from java.lang.Exception (except RuntimeException)
  • Must be either caught or declared in the method signature
  • Used for recoverable conditions
  • Examples: IOException, SQLException, ParseException

public void readFile(String filePath) throws IOException {
    BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(filePath));
    // read file...
}
⚠️ Unchecked Exceptions
  • Inherit from java.lang.RuntimeException
  • No need to catch or declare in method signature
  • Used for programming errors like logic mistakes or improper API use
  • Examples: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, IllegalArgumentException 

public void printLength(String input) {
    System.out.println(input.length()); // may throw NullPointerException
}
✅ Summary
Aspect Checked Unchecked
Inheritance Exception RuntimeException
Handled/Declared? Yes No
Common Usage Recoverable errors Programming errors
Examples IOException, SQLException NullPointerException, IllegalStateException

✅ Common & Essential String Methods
  • length() – Returns the length of the string
  • charAt(int index) – Returns the character at the specified index
  • substring(int begin, int end) – Returns a substring
  • equals(Object obj) – Compares content of strings
  • equalsIgnoreCase(String another) – Case-insensitive equality check
  • compareTo(String another) – Lexicographically compares two strings
  • contains(CharSequence s) – Checks if a string contains a sequence
  • indexOf(String str) – Returns index of first occurrence
  • toLowerCase() / toUpperCase() – Case transformation
  • replace(CharSequence target, CharSequence replacement) – Replaces characters
  • split(String regex) – Splits string around matches
  • trim() – Removes leading/trailing whitespaces
✨ Java 11+ String Methods
  • isBlank() – Returns true if string is empty or contains only white space
  • lines() – Returns a stream of lines from the string
  • repeat(int count) – Returns a string repeated count times
  • strip() – Removes leading/trailing whitespaces (Unicode-aware, better than trim())
  • stripLeading() – Removes leading whitespaces
  • stripTrailing() – Removes trailing whitespaces

// Java 11+ Example
String text = "  Hello World  \nWelcome to Java!";
System.out.println(text.strip());               // Removes spaces
System.out.println(text.lines().count());       // Counts lines
System.out.println("Java".repeat(3));           // JavaJavaJava
System.out.println("  ".isBlank());             // true
🧠 Tips
  • Prefer isBlank() over trim().isEmpty()
  • Use strip() instead of trim() for Unicode whitespace
  • Use repeat() for padding or repeating strings easily

🔒 Private Methods in Interface (Since Java 9)
  • Used to share common code between default and static methods.
