  • Large volumes of rapidly changing, semi-structured/unstructured data
  • Need for horizontal scaling and high availability
  • Flexible schema, distributed architecture, fast read/writes
  • Real-time analytics, IoT, big data, personalization engines
🌍 Popular Companies Using NoSQL
  • Facebook – Cassandra for messaging and feed systems
  • Netflix – Cassandra and Redis for scalability
  • Amazon – DynamoDB for shopping cart, personalization
  • Google – BigTable (infrastructure for Gmail, Maps)
  • LinkedIn – Voldemort, Espresso, and Kafka
  • Uber – Riak, Schemaless (built on MySQL + NoSQL style)
📌 Summary

Choose SQL for well-structured data, consistency, and transactional support. Go with NoSQL for flexibility, high scalability, and performance in modern data-heavy applications like real-time analytics or large-scale distributed systems.

📌 What are Annotations in Spring Boot?

In Spring Boot, annotations are used to configure beans, define request mappings, inject dependencies, and much more. They help reduce XML configuration and enable a cleaner, declarative programming model.

Think of them as instructions for the Spring Framework to wire and manage your application components.

✅ Common Annotations in Spring Boot
  • @SpringBootApplication – Bootstraps the application
  • @RestController – Creates a RESTful controller
  • @Autowired – Injects dependencies
  • @RequestMapping – Maps HTTP requests to methods
  • @Component, @Service, @Repository – Mark Spring-managed classes
📌 Why Create a Custom Annotation?

Sometimes, you want to group common behavior into a single, reusable annotation. For example, combining multiple Spring annotations or marking special business logic methods.

✅ How to Create a Custom Annotation in Spring Boot

import java.lang.annotation.*;

@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
public @interface LogExecutionTime {
}

Here, we created a custom annotation called @LogExecutionTime that can be applied to methods.

📌 How to Use the Custom Annotation with Aspect (AOP)

Now let's use Spring AOP to define behavior when this annotation is used:


import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Around;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect;
import org.aspectj.lang.ProceedingJoinPoint;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Aspect
@Component
public class LogExecutionAspect {

    @Around("@annotation(LogExecutionTime)")
    public Object logExecutionTime(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
        Object proceed = joinPoint.proceed();
        long duration = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;
        System.out.println(joinPoint.getSignature() + " executed in " + duration + "ms");
        return proceed;
    }
}
✅ Using the Custom Annotation in a Service

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class MyService {

    @LogExecutionTime
    public void serve() throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(1000);
        System.out.println("Service Method Executed");
    }
}
📌 Full Spring Boot App Example

// Main Application
@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ConfigurableApplicationContext context = SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
        MyService myService = context.getBean(MyService.class);
        myService.serve();
    }
}
🔔 Notes
  • AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming) allows cross-cutting concerns like logging or transactions.
  • Spring handles the annotation scanning and applies behavior at runtime.
  • Custom annotations + AOP = Powerful abstraction for repeated logic.
✅ Benefits of Custom Annotations
  • 👉 Cleaner and reusable code
  • 👉 Group multiple behaviors into one label
  • 👉 Encourage declarative programming style
  • 👉 Makes your codebase more expressive and self-documented
📢 Summary

Custom annotations in Spring Boot 3 let you create expressive, reusable, and declarative components. Combined with Spring AOP, they help implement behaviors like logging, validation, or security checks cleanly and consistently.

📌 What is a Bean Scope in Spring?

Bean scope defines the lifecycle and visibility of a bean in Spring. Common scopes include:

  • singleton – one instance for the entire application context
  • prototype – a new instance every time it’s requested
  • request/session – tied to web request/session

Custom scopes are useful when you want more control – like one bean per thread, task, etc.

✅ Step 1: Create the Custom Scope

We’ll create a ThreadScope which gives each thread its own bean instance.


import org.springframework.beans.factory.ObjectFactory;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.config.Scope;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class ThreadScope implements Scope {

    private final ThreadLocal<Map<String, Object>> threadScope = ThreadLocal.withInitial(HashMap::new);

    @Override
    public Object get(String name, ObjectFactory<?> objectFactory) {
        return threadScope.get().computeIfAbsent(name, k -> objectFactory.getObject());
    }

    @Override
    public Object remove(String name) {
        return threadScope.get().remove(name);
    }

    @Override
    public void registerDestructionCallback(String name, Runnable callback) {
        // Not required for thread scope
    }

    @Override
    public Object resolveContextualObject(String key) {
        return null;
    }

    @Override
    public String getConversationId() {
        return Thread.currentThread().getName();
    }
}
📌 Step 2: Register the Custom Scope

import org.springframework.beans.factory.config.ConfigurableBeanFactory;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration
public class ScopeConfig {

    @Bean
    public static org.springframework.beans.factory.config.CustomScopeConfigurer customScopeConfigurer() {
        org.springframework.beans.factory.config.CustomScopeConfigurer configurer = new org.springframework.beans.factory.config.CustomScopeConfigurer();
        configurer.addScope("thread", new ThreadScope());
        return configurer;
    }
}
✅ Step 3: Create a Bean with the Custom Scope

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Scope;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
@Scope("thread")
public class ThreadScopedBean {
    public ThreadScopedBean() {
        System.out.println("ThreadScopedBean created for " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}
📌 Step 4: Use the Scoped Bean

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class DemoRunner implements CommandLineRunner {

    @Autowired
    private org.springframework.context.ApplicationContext context;

    @Override
    public void run(String... args) {
        Runnable task = () -> {
            ThreadScopedBean bean1 = context.getBean(ThreadScopedBean.class);
            ThreadScopedBean bean2 = context.getBean(ThreadScopedBean.class);
            System.out.println("Same instance in same thread? " + (bean1 == bean2));
        };

        Thread t1 = new Thread(task, "Thread-A");
        Thread t2 = new Thread(task, "Thread-B");

        t1.start();
        t2.start();
    }
}
🔔 Output

ThreadScopedBean created for Thread-A
ThreadScopedBean created for Thread-B
Same instance in same thread? true
Same instance in same thread? true
✅ Summary
  • 👉 You can define your own bean lifecycle with a custom scope.
  • 👉 Useful for thread-bound beans, jobs, or temporary states.
  • 👉 Spring makes it easy to register and use via `CustomScopeConfigurer`.

Conclusion: Custom scopes allow powerful, flexible control over bean management in Spring Boot 3 applications!

📌 What is Caching?

Caching is a technique to store frequently used data in memory so it can be retrieved faster. Spring Boot makes it easy to add caching with just annotations!

Use Case: Avoid hitting database or API repeatedly for the same data.

✅ Common Cache Annotations in Spring
  • @EnableCaching – Enables Spring's cache abstraction
  • @Cacheable – Marks a method whose result should be cached
  • @CacheEvict – Marks a method that should clear cache
  • @CachePut – Updates the cache without skipping method execution
📌 Step 1: Add Redis Dependencies (Maven)

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
</dependency>
✅ Step 2: Add Redis Configuration (application.yml)

spring:
  cache:
    type: redis
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost
      port: 6379
      timeout: 6000
      password: yourRedisPassword # Optional if no auth
      client-type: lettuce
      lettuce:
        pool:
          max-active: 8
          max-idle: 8
          min-idle: 0
📌 Step 3: Enable Caching in Main Class

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.cache.annotation.EnableCaching;

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableCaching
public class DemoApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}
✅ Step 4: Create a Caching Service

import org.springframework.cache.annotation.Cacheable;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class ProductService {

    @Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#id")
    public String getProductById(String id) {
        System.out.println("Fetching from DB for ID: " + id);
        return "Product-" + id;
    }
}
📌 Step 5: Test the Cache (Controller)

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/products")
public class ProductController {

    private final ProductService productService;

    public ProductController(ProductService productService) {
        this.productService = productService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public String getProduct(@PathVariable String id) {
        return productService.getProductById(id);
    }
}
🔁 What Happens on Repeated Calls?

The first call to /products/123 will fetch from DB (simulated), and the second call will return instantly from Redis cache.

✅ Cache Eviction Example

@CacheEvict(value = "products", key = "#id")
public void clearCache(String id) {
    System.out.println("Cache cleared for product: " + id);
}
🔔 Redis Running?
  • 👉 Make sure Redis is running on your machine or use Docker
  • 👉 Docker Command: docker run -p 6379:6379 redis
  • 👉 RedisInsight GUI can help you view cached keys
✅ Summary
  • 👉 Add Redis dependency & config
  • 👉 Enable caching with @EnableCaching
  • 👉 Annotate methods with @Cacheable
  • 👉 Cache data externally in Redis for scalability

Conclusion: Externalizing cache with Redis in Spring Boot 3 is simple, powerful, and production-ready!

📌 What is Inter-Microservice Communication?

In a microservice architecture, multiple services must communicate to fulfill a business request. This communication can happen in two main ways: synchronously or asynchronously.

✅ 1. Synchronous Communication (HTTP/REST, gRPC, Feign)
  • 👉 The client waits for a response from the server
  • 👉 Works like traditional request-response pattern
🔹 a) REST using `RestTemplate` / `WebClient`

@RestController
public class OrderController {
    @Autowired
    private RestTemplate restTemplate;

    @GetMapping("/order")
    public String placeOrder() {
        String product = restTemplate.getForObject("http://product-service/product/123", String.class);
        return "Order placed for " + product;
    }
}
🔹 b) Feign Client (Declarative HTTP Client)

@FeignClient(name = "product-service")
public interface ProductClient {
    @GetMapping("/product/{id}")
    String getProduct(@PathVariable String id);
}
🔹 c) gRPC (Binary-based, Faster Communication)

Used for high-performance communication with Protobuf. More efficient than REST but adds complexity.

⚖️ Advantages of Synchronous
  • ✅ Simple to implement and debug
  • ✅ Easy error handling and retries
  • ✅ Suitable for direct dependencies
❌ Disadvantages of Synchronous
  • ❌ Tight coupling between services
  • ❌ Latency increases with each chained call
  • ❌ Hard to scale under load (blocking I/O)
✅ 2. Asynchronous Communication (Message Queues, Kafka, RabbitMQ)
  • 👉 Services communicate via events/messages
  • 👉 The sender doesn't wait for a response
🔹 a) RabbitMQ Example (Spring Boot)

// Producer
rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend("order.exchange", "order.created", order);

// Consumer
@RabbitListener(queues = "order.queue")
public void processOrder(Order order) {
    System.out.println("Order received: " + order);
}
🔹 b) Kafka Example

// Kafka Producer
kafkaTemplate.send("order-topic", orderId, orderDetails);

// Kafka Listener
@KafkaListener(topics = "order-topic")
public void handleOrder(String order) {
    System.out.println("Received order via Kafka: " + order);
}
⚖️ Advantages of Asynchronous
  • ✅ Loose coupling between services
  • ✅ Highly scalable and resilient
  • ✅ Handles high traffic well (non-blocking)
❌ Disadvantages of Asynchronous
  • ❌ More complex to implement and monitor
  • ❌ Harder to debug and trace issues
  • ❌ Eventual consistency (not immediate)
📌 Which One Should You Use?
  • 👉 Use REST/gRPC for quick, real-time responses and simpler services
  • 👉 Use Kafka/RabbitMQ when performance, decoupling, and resilience are top priorities
  • 👉 A combination of both is common in modern systems (hybrid model)
✅ Summary
  • 🔄 Synchronous: REST, gRPC, Feign – good for request-response, but tightly coupled
  • 📩 Asynchronous: Kafka, RabbitMQ – better for decoupling, scaling, and resilience
  • ⚙️ Choose based on use case: real-time needs vs. throughput & flexibility

📌 What is Auto-Configuration in Spring Boot?

Spring Boot auto-configures many things for you based on the classpath and configuration files. This is done using the @SpringBootApplication and underlying @EnableAutoConfiguration.

Auto-configurations are provided via spring-boot-autoconfigure module using conditions like @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnProperty, etc.

✅ Why Customize Auto-Configuration?
  • 👉 You want to override or replace a default bean
  • 👉 You want to enable or disable features conditionally
  • 👉 You want full control over how something is configured
📌 1. Override Default Auto-Configured Beans

@Configuration
public class CustomDataSourceConfig {

    @Bean
    @Primary
    public DataSource customDataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create()
                .url("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/customdb")
                .username("root")
                .password("root")
                .build();
    }
}

✅ Spring will use this instead of the default DataSource due to @Primary.

✅ 2. Use Conditional Configuration

@Configuration
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "app.custom.enabled", havingValue = "true")
public class MyCustomFeature {

    @Bean
    public MyService myService() {
        return new MyService();
    }
}

✅ This bean will only be loaded if app.custom.enabled=true is set in application.properties.

📌 3. Disable a Specific Auto-Configuration

@SpringBootApplication(exclude = { DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class })
public class MyApp { ... }

✅ Use exclude or excludeName to block certain auto-configs.

✅ 4. Create Your Own Auto-Configuration

// MyLibraryAutoConfiguration.java
@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass(MyLibrary.class)
public class MyLibraryAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    public MyLibrary myLibrary() {
        return new MyLibrary();
    }
}
      

# META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
com.example.config.MyLibraryAutoConfiguration

✅ This registers your config as a valid auto-configuration class in Spring Boot 3 (replaces older spring.factories).

🔍 Use Auto-Configuration Report for Debugging

Set this in application.properties:


debug=true

✅ This prints which auto-configs were applied or not, and why.

✅ Summary
  • 🔧 Customize by overriding beans or using conditions
  • 🛠️ Disable auto-config classes you don’t want
  • 📦 You can also create and share your own auto-config modules
  • 📊 Use debug=true for full config insights

Conclusion: Spring Boot gives you powerful ways to override or plug into the auto-configuration system with minimal effort and full control.

📌 What is a Service Registry?

A Service Registry is a **central database** or server that keeps track of all **available services** in a microservice ecosystem.

When a new microservice starts up, it registers its information (host, port, metadata) to the registry.

✅ Example: Eureka Server

# application.yml of service
eureka:
  client:
    register-with-eureka: true
    fetch-registry: true
    service-url:
      defaultZone: http://localhost:8761/eureka

Here, each service registers itself with the central Eureka registry.

🎯 Purpose:
  • 👉 Keep track of all services in the system
  • 👉 Maintain metadata like name, IP, port, health status
📌 What is Service Discovery?

Service Discovery is the **process of locating the address of a service** using the service registry.

Instead of hardcoding service URLs, services can dynamically discover others via the registry.

✅ Example: Using Eureka Discovery Client

@Autowired
private DiscoveryClient discoveryClient;

public String callAnotherService() {
    List instances = 
        discoveryClient.getInstances("user-service");
    URI uri = instances.get(0).getUri();
    return restTemplate.getForObject(uri + "/api/users", String.class);
}

✅ This code dynamically discovers a running instance of user-service.

🎯 Purpose:
  • 👉 Locate services dynamically at runtime
  • 👉 Enable client-side or server-side load balancing
  • 👉 Remove the need for hardcoded URLs
📌 Real-World Analogy
  • 🗂️ Service Registry = Phone Directory
  • 📞 Service Discovery = Looking up a friend’s phone number before calling
✅ Key Differences
Aspect Service Registry Service Discovery
Definition Central storage of service metadata Mechanism to look up available services
Responsibility Maintain list of running service instances Find and connect to services using that list
Examples Eureka Server, Consul, Zookeeper DiscoveryClient, Feign + Eureka, Ribbon, Consul client
Who Uses It? All services register themselves to it Clients/services query it to find other services
Analogy Phonebook Looking up a number in phonebook
📌 Types of Service Discovery
  • 🔹 Client-side Discovery (e.g., Eureka + Ribbon): Client queries registry and chooses instance
  • 🔹 Server-side Discovery (e.g., AWS ELB, Kubernetes): Load balancer queries registry and routes traffic
✅ Summary
  • 🛠️ Service Registry is the **data source** of service locations
  • 🔍 Service Discovery is the **mechanism** of finding services from that source
  • 🔗 Both are essential in **dynamic and scalable microservice architectures**

📌 What is Saga Design Pattern?

The Saga pattern is a **distributed transaction pattern** used in microservices to manage **data consistency** across multiple services **without using a distributed transaction coordinator**.

It breaks a transaction into a sequence of **local transactions**, each updating one microservice and publishing an event or invoking the next step.

🔄 Key Idea:
  • Each service **executes its transaction** and then triggers the next via events or direct calls.
  • If something fails, Saga pattern triggers **compensating transactions** to undo changes.
📚 Real-world Example: Order Placement
  • 1️⃣ Order Service: Creates the order
  • 2️⃣ Payment Service: Deducts the payment
  • 3️⃣ Inventory Service: Reduces stock
  • 4️⃣ Shipping Service: Initiates delivery

If Inventory fails, Saga will rollback Payment and Order.

📌 Types of Saga
1. Choreography-based Saga

There is **no central orchestrator**. Each service listens for events and responds accordingly.


OrderService → emits OrderCreatedEvent
↓
PaymentService → listens to OrderCreatedEvent, processes payment, emits PaymentCompletedEvent
↓
InventoryService → listens to PaymentCompletedEvent, updates stock, emits StockUpdatedEvent
↓
ShippingService → listens to StockUpdatedEvent, ships item

🚫 If one fails, the failing service emits a compensating event like PaymentFailedEvent.

✅ Pros:
  • ✅ No single point of failure
  • ✅ Decoupled services via events
⚠️ Cons:
  • ⚠️ Harder to monitor and debug
  • ⚠️ Complex failure handling logic
2. Orchestration-based Saga

A central **Saga orchestrator** (like a workflow engine) tells each service what to do and coordinates the saga.


public class OrderSagaOrchestrator {

  public void startSaga(Order order) {
    orderService.create(order);
    paymentService.pay(order.getId());
    inventoryService.reserve(order.getId());
    shippingService.ship(order.getId());
  }

  public void compensate(Order order) {
    shippingService.cancel(order.getId());
    inventoryService.release(order.getId());
    paymentService.refund(order.getId());
    orderService.cancel(order.getId());
  }
}
✅ Pros:
  • ✅ Centralized flow control
  • ✅ Easier to monitor and debug
⚠️ Cons:
  • ⚠️ Orchestrator is a single point of failure
  • ⚠️ Can become tightly coupled
📌 Compensating Transactions

These are reverse operations to undo what a failed step did. For example:

  • ✅ Refund payment
  • ✅ Restock inventory
  • ✅ Cancel order
📢 Saga Implementation Tools
  • 🛠️ Choreography: Spring Boot + Kafka / RabbitMQ
  • 🛠️ Orchestration: Camunda, Netflix Conductor, Axon Framework, Temporal
✅ Summary
  • 🧩 Saga ensures **eventual consistency** in distributed systems
  • 🔄 Supports **rollback via compensating actions**
  • ⚙️ Two styles: **Choreography** (event-driven) and **Orchestration** (central controller)
  • ✅ Ideal for business transactions spanning multiple microservices

📌 What is Idempotency?

Idempotency is the property of an operation where **executing it multiple times** has the **same effect** as executing it once.

This means: f(f(x)) = f(x). It’s critical in **distributed systems** to ensure **reliability** and **safe retries**.

✅ Why is Idempotency Important?
  • 🔁 Retries due to network failures or timeouts
  • 📨 Duplicate API requests from client/browser
  • ⚙️ Safe operations during load balancing or failover
📚 Real-world Analogy
  • 🧾 Pushing an elevator button multiple times → only one action: the elevator arrives (idempotent)
  • 💳 Making the same bank transfer twice → should not happen (non-idempotent unless protected)
📌 Idempotent vs Non-Idempotent HTTP Methods
HTTP Method Idempotent? Reason
GET ✅ Yes Read-only, no side effects
PUT ✅ Yes Same resource state is set repeatedly
DELETE ✅ Yes Multiple deletes are still safe
POST ❌ No Creates new resources (can cause duplicates)
✅ How to Implement Idempotency in Microservices?
  • 🔑 Use Idempotency-Key header from clients (UUID per request)
  • 🧠 Store this key in a DB/cache with response
  • 🔁 If same key is received again, return stored response instead of executing again
🔧 Example (Spring Boot)

@PostMapping("/payments")
public ResponseEntity makePayment(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key) {
    if (paymentService.existsByKey(key)) {
        return paymentService.getResponseByKey(key);
    }
    PaymentResponse response = paymentService.processPayment();
    paymentService.storeKeyAndResponse(key, response);
    return ResponseEntity.ok(response);
}
📢 Best Practices
  • ✅ Enforce idempotency for all POST requests that mutate state
  • ✅ Use database or Redis for idempotency key storage
  • ⚠️ Set expiration time for keys to avoid memory issues
✅ Summary
  • 🔁 Idempotency ensures **safe retries** of operations in distributed systems
  • 🔐 Helps in avoiding duplicate actions like double payments or repeated orders
  • 🛠️ Can be implemented using **unique request keys** and **response caching**
  • ✅ A critical pattern for **reliable microservices** and **REST APIs**

📌 What is Idempotency?

Idempotency is a property of an operation where **executing it multiple times** has the **same effect** as executing it once. This means: f(f(x)) = f(x). It is an important concept in distributed systems to ensure **safe retries** and **reliable operations**.

✅ Key Points:
  • 🔁 **No side effects** on repeated execution
  • 📈 Ensures that multiple invocations result in **the same outcome**
📚 Real-World Analogy
  • 🚪 **Pressing a doorbell** multiple times results in the same action: bell rings (no change in outcome).
  • 💳 **Making a bank transfer** multiple times may lead to multiple charges (not idempotent unless handled).
📌 Idempotent HTTP Methods

Certain HTTP methods are **idempotent** by nature:

HTTP Method Idempotent? Reason
GET ✅ Yes Fetching data doesn’t change the resource
PUT ✅ Yes Re-setting a resource’s value results in the same value
DELETE ✅ Yes Deleting a resource multiple times has the same effect (resource is gone)
POST ❌ No Creating resources (multiple POST requests may create duplicates)
✅ Example of Idempotency in APIs

@PostMapping("/payments")
public ResponseEntity makePayment(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key) {
    if (paymentService.existsByKey(key)) {
        return paymentService.getResponseByKey(key);
    }
    PaymentResponse response = paymentService.processPayment();
    paymentService.storeKeyAndResponse(key, response);
    return ResponseEntity.ok(response);
}
🔑 Key Idea:
  • Each request has a unique **Idempotency-Key** (UUID) to identify it.
  • If the same key is sent again, the same response is returned without re-executing the transaction.
✅ Benefits of Idempotency
  • 🔒 **Avoid duplicate transactions** (like double payments or orders)
  • ⚙️ **Safe retries** in distributed systems (e.g., network failure)
  • 💡 Helps in building **reliable and fault-tolerant** APIs
📢 Summary
  • 🔄 **Idempotent operations** produce the same outcome even if invoked multiple times.
  • ✅ Ensures that **distributed systems** are robust and prevent unintended side effects.
  • 💡 Can be implemented using unique **Idempotency keys** to track requests.

📌 The Superclass of All Java Classes

The superclass of every Java class is the Object class. It is the **root** class in Java's class hierarchy.

Every class in Java, whether explicitly or implicitly, inherits from the Object class.

✅ Why is Object the Superclass?
  • 🔑 It provides fundamental methods to all Java objects, such as toString(), equals(), and hashCode().
  • 📚 All Java classes, by default, inherit from this class, even if you don’t explicitly extend it.
📌 Methods Provided by Object Class
  • toString(): Returns a string representation of the object.
  • equals(): Compares the current object with another object for equality.
  • hashCode(): Returns a hash code value for the object.
  • getClass(): Returns the runtime class of the object.
  • clone(): Creates and returns a copy of the object (if the class implements Cloneable).
📚 Example

public class MyClass {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MyClass myObject = new MyClass();
        
        // All objects in Java inherit methods from Object class
        System.out.println(myObject.toString());  // Calls Object's toString method
        System.out.println(myObject.getClass());  // Calls Object's getClass method
    }
}
Output:

MyClass@5e2b9f3b
class MyClass
✅ Key Takeaway
  • 🔄 Every class in Java inherits from the Object class, even if not explicitly extended.
  • ⚙️ The Object class provides essential methods like toString() and equals(), making them available to all Java objects.

📌 Overview of OOP Principles

In Java, the key **Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)** principles are:

  • **Polymorphism**
  • **Inheritance**
  • **Abstraction**
  • **Encapsulation**
✅ 1. **Polymorphism**

Polymorphism allows objects to be treated as instances of their parent class, enabling one interface to represent different underlying forms (methods).

In simple terms: The same method can behave differently based on the object that calls it.

Example:

class Animal {
    void makeSound() {
        System.out.println("Animal sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void makeSound() {
        System.out.println("Bark");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal myDog = new Dog(); // Polymorphism
        myDog.makeSound();  // Output: Bark
    }
}

Here, **Polymorphism** is demonstrated because the method makeSound() behaves differently for Dog and Animal.

✅ 2. **Inheritance**

Inheritance allows one class (child class) to inherit fields and methods from another class (parent class). This promotes code reuse.

Example:

class Animal {
    void eat() {
        System.out.println("Eating");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    void bark() {
        System.out.println("Barking");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog dog = new Dog();
        dog.eat();  // Inherited from Animal
        dog.bark(); // Defined in Dog
    }
}

Here, the **Dog** class inherits the eat() method from the **Animal** class, demonstrating **Inheritance**.

✅ 3. **Abstraction**

Abstraction hides the complex implementation details and shows only the essential features of an object. In Java, abstraction is achieved using **abstract classes** and **interfaces**.

Example (Abstract Class):

abstract class Animal {
    abstract void makeSound();  // Abstract method
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void makeSound() {
        System.out.println("Bark");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal myDog = new Dog();
        myDog.makeSound(); // Output: Bark
    }
}

Here, **Abstraction** is demonstrated because the makeSound() method is abstract in the **Animal** class and implemented in the **Dog** class.

✅ 4. **Encapsulation**

Encapsulation is the bundling of data (variables) and methods (functions) that operate on the data into a single unit or class. It also restricts direct access to some of an object's components, which is why it’s used to hide the internal object state.

Example:

class Person {
    private String name;  // Private field

    public String getName() { // Getter
        return name;
    }

    public void setName(String name) { // Setter
        this.name = name;
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Person person = new Person();
        person.setName("John");  // Encapsulation: Using setter
        System.out.println(person.getName());  // Encapsulation: Using getter
    }
}

Here, **Encapsulation** is demonstrated because the name field is private and can only be accessed or modified using public getter and setter methods.

📢 Summary of All OOP Principles:
  • 🔄 **Polymorphism**: Same method, different behavior.
  • 🔗 **Inheritance**: Child class inherits features from the parent class.
  • 🧑‍💻 **Abstraction**: Hides complexity, only shows essential features.
  • 🔒 **Encapsulation**: Hides internal state, and only allows access through methods.

📌 Problem Overview

You have an array with duplicate elements, and you need to remove the duplicates while preserving the order of elements as they originally appeared.

✅ Approach

In Java, we can use a **LinkedHashSet** because it allows us to maintain the insertion order while removing duplicates. A **HashSet** would remove duplicates but not maintain order.

🔑 Key Concept: LinkedHashSet
  • 🔗 **LinkedHashSet** is a collection that combines the functionality of a HashSet (removes duplicates) and a linked list (preserves insertion order).
  • 📜 The order of elements is maintained by a **LinkedHashSet**.
📌 Example Code

import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.Arrays;

public class RemoveDuplicates {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Input array with duplicates
        Integer[] arr = {1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 1, 6, 4};
        
        // Using LinkedHashSet to remove duplicates and maintain insertion order
        LinkedHashSet set = new LinkedHashSet<>(Arrays.asList(arr));
        
        // Converting the set back to an array
        Integer[] result = set.toArray(new Integer[0]);
        
        // Output the result
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(result));  // Output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
    }
}
✅ Explanation of Code
  • 💻 We initialize a **LinkedHashSet** with the array elements to remove duplicates.
  • 🔄 The elements of the set are automatically ordered based on their first occurrence.
  • 📜 We then convert the set back to an array using toArray() to maintain the order.
📢 Output

[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

The duplicates have been removed, and the order of the elements is preserved from the original array.

✅ Key Takeaways
  • 🔄 **LinkedHashSet** is used to remove duplicates and maintain the insertion order.
  • ⚡ The time complexity for this operation is approximately O(n), where n is the number of elements in the array.
  • 🔄 This method is simple and efficient for removing duplicates in an array while preserving the order.

📌 What is the `transient` Keyword?

The `transient` keyword in Java is used to indicate that a field should not be serialized. Serialization is the process of converting an object into a byte stream for saving or transferring it. When a field is marked as transient, it will not be included in the serialization process.

✅ Use Case of `transient` Keyword
  • 🔒 **Security**: Sensitive data (like passwords) should be marked as transient to avoid being serialized.
  • 💾 **Performance**: Some fields might be temporary and not needed for persistence, so they can be marked transient.
📌 Default Value of Transient Fields

When a field is marked as transient, its default value will depend on the type of the field.

📜 Default Values:
  • For primitive types: The default value will be the default value of the primitive type (e.g., 0 for int, false for boolean).
  • For wrapper classes (like Integer, Double): The default value will be null.
✅ Example: `transient` with Primitives and Wrapper Classes

import java.io.*;

class Person implements Serializable {
    String name;
    transient int age;  // 'age' will not be serialized
    transient Integer id;  // 'id' will not be serialized
    
    public Person(String name, int age, Integer id) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
        this.id = id;
    }
}

public class TestTransient {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
        // Creating an object
        Person person = new Person("John", 30, 12345);

        // Serialize the object to a file
        FileOutputStream fileOut = new FileOutputStream("person.ser");
        ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(fileOut);
        out.writeObject(person);
        out.close();

        // Deserialize the object from the file
        FileInputStream fileIn = new FileInputStream("person.ser");
        ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(fileIn);
        Person deserializedPerson = (Person) in.readObject();
        in.close();

        // Display the object fields after deserialization
        System.out.println("Name: " + deserializedPerson.name);  // Output: John
        System.out.println("Age: " + deserializedPerson.age);    // Output: 0 (default for int)
        System.out.println("ID: " + deserializedPerson.id);      // Output: null (default for Integer)
    }
}
📌 Explanation of Example
  • 📁 **Serialization**: The Person object is serialized to a file.
  • ⚡ **Deserialization**: After deserialization, the age and id fields are restored to their default values. Since they are marked as transient, they are not serialized and hence have their default values:
    • **`age`** (primitive int): 0 (default value for int)
    • **`id`** (wrapper Integer): null (default value for reference types)
📢 Key Takeaways
  • 🛑 The transient keyword prevents a field from being serialized.
  • 🔄 After deserialization, fields marked as transient will have their default values, depending on whether they are primitive or wrapper types.
  • ⚡ For primitive fields like int, the default is 0, and for wrapper classes like Integer, the default is null.

📌 What Are `StringBuilder` and `StringBuffer`?

Both StringBuilder and StringBuffer are used to create mutable strings in Java. Unlike the String class, which is immutable, these classes allow modification of the string without creating a new object each time.

✅ Key Differences
  • 🔒 **Thread Safety**:
    • StringBuffer is **synchronized** and thread-safe. Multiple threads can safely modify a StringBuffer object.
    • StringBuilder is **not synchronized** and not thread-safe. It is faster than StringBuffer in a single-threaded environment.
  • ⚡ **Performance**:
    • StringBuilder is faster than StringBuffer because it doesn't have the overhead of synchronization.
    • StringBuffer has slower performance due to synchronization, which adds a cost when used in multi-threaded environments.
  • 🔄 **Synchronization**:
    • StringBuffer guarantees thread-safety by synchronizing methods, making it suitable for concurrent modifications.
    • StringBuilder does not synchronize methods, and thus it is not thread-safe, but it is ideal for single-threaded scenarios.
🔑 When to Use Each?
  • 💡 Use **StringBuilder** when thread safety is not required (i.e., in single-threaded applications), as it offers better performance.
  • 🔒 Use **StringBuffer** when thread safety is required (i.e., in multi-threaded applications), but keep in mind the performance overhead.
📌 Example Code

public class StringBuilderVsStringBuffer {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Using StringBuffer (thread-safe)
        StringBuffer buffer = new StringBuffer("Hello");
        buffer.append(" World");
        System.out.println("StringBuffer: " + buffer);  // Output: Hello World

        // Using StringBuilder (not thread-safe)
        StringBuilder builder = new StringBuilder("Hello");
        builder.append(" World");
        System.out.println("StringBuilder: " + builder);  // Output: Hello World
    }
}
✅ Output

StringBuffer: Hello World
StringBuilder: Hello World

Both StringBuffer and StringBuilder work similarly for string manipulation, but the difference lies in thread-safety and performance.

📢 Key Takeaways
  • 🔄 **StringBuilder** is faster and suitable for single-threaded environments.
  • 🔒 **StringBuffer** is thread-safe but slower due to synchronization, making it ideal for multi-threaded environments.
  • ⚡ Choose the class based on your application's need for thread safety and performance requirements.

📌 What is `==` in Java?

The == operator is used to compare **memory references** (or object addresses) of two objects. For primitive types, it compares the actual values. It checks if two variables point to the same memory location.

✅ What is `equals()` in Java?

The equals() method is used to compare **values** of two objects. It is defined in the Object class, and can be overridden to compare object contents rather than their memory references.

🔑 Key Differences Between `==` and `equals()`
  • 💡 **`==`**:
    • Compares memory reference (for objects) or actual values (for primitives).
    • For objects, it checks if both variables point to the same memory location.
    • For primitives, it compares the values directly.
  • 💡 **`equals()`**:
    • Compares the **contents** or values of the objects.
    • It can be overridden to define custom equality logic for specific classes.
    • By default, it behaves like == (in Object class), but it is often overridden in custom classes to compare values.
📌 Behavior for Wrapper and Literal Classes

The behavior of == and equals() differs for wrapper classes (like Integer, Double) and literal strings due to **Java caching mechanisms** and **autoboxing**.

✅ Example with Wrapper Classes

public class EqualsVsDoubleEquals {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Integer x = 100;
        Integer y = 100;
        Integer z = 200;
        Integer w = 200;

        // Using ==
        System.out.println(x == y);  // true (because of caching for values between -128 and 127)
        System.out.println(z == w);  // false (new objects are created)

        // Using equals()
        System.out.println(x.equals(y));  // true (values are the same)
        System.out.println(z.equals(w));  // true (values are the same)
    }
}
📜 Explanation for Wrapper Classes
  • For **Integer** values in the range of -128 to 127, Java **caches** them. So, for 100, both x and y point to the same object in memory. Thus, x == y is true.
  • For **Integer** values outside the range of -128 to 127 (like 200), == compares memory references, and thus returns false because new objects are created for z and w.
  • However, equals() compares the values of the wrapper objects, so x.equals(y) and z.equals(w) return true because their values are the same.
✅ Example with String Literals

public class StringLiteralExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String str1 = "Hello";
        String str2 = "Hello";
        String str3 = new String("Hello");

        // Using ==
        System.out.println(str1 == str2);  // true (both refer to the same memory location)
        System.out.println(str1 == str3);  // false (str3 is a new object)

        // Using equals()
        System.out.println(str1.equals(str2));  // true (values are the same)
        System.out.println(str1.equals(str3));  // true (values are the same)
    }
}
📜 Explanation for String Literals
  • For **String literals**, Java maintains a **String pool** where it stores only one copy of each unique string literal. So, both str1 and str2 refer to the same memory location, and str1 == str2 is true.
  • However, when using the new keyword, like new String("Hello"), a new object is created on the heap. Therefore, str1 == str3 is false, even though the content is the same.
  • equals() compares the content of strings, so str1.equals(str2) and str1.equals(str3) both return true, as the values are the same.
📌 Key Takeaways
  • 🔄 **`==`** compares memory references (for objects) or actual values (for primitives).
  • 🔄 **`equals()`** compares the values of objects and can be overridden in custom classes.
  • ⚡ For **wrapper classes** (like Integer), == compares memory locations, and values within the range of -128 to 127 are cached.
  • ⚡ For **String literals**, == works because of the **String pool** and string interning, but new String() creates a new object.

📌 What is an Index in SQL?

An **index** in SQL is a database object that **improves the speed** of data retrieval operations on a table at the cost of additional space and time for insertions, updates, and deletions.

Indexes are created on one or more columns of a table to speed up the search operations. They are similar to the index in a book where you can quickly look up a term instead of reading through the entire book.

✅ How Does an Index Work?

When an index is created on a table, it builds a data structure, typically a **B-tree** (or variations like **hash index**, **bitmap index** depending on the DBMS), that allows for fast retrieval of rows based on the indexed column(s).

  • The index stores the values from the column(s) in a sorted order, along with pointers to the corresponding rows in the table.
  • This sorting allows the database to quickly perform **binary search** or similar fast lookup algorithms on the index structure, instead of scanning the entire table.
🔑 Advantages of Using Indexes
  • ⚡ **Faster Queries**: Especially for SELECT queries with WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY clauses.
  • ⚡ **Improved Sorting**: Indexes allow the database to quickly sort data.
  • ⚡ **Efficient Joins**: Indexes improve performance in join operations by quickly finding matching rows.
❗ Disadvantages of Using Indexes
  • ⚠️ **Slower Insert, Update, and Delete**: When data is modified, the index also needs to be updated, which adds overhead.
  • ⚠️ **Increased Storage**: Indexes consume additional disk space, especially if created on multiple columns.
📌 Creating an Index in SQL

You can create an index using the CREATE INDEX statement. Below is an example:


-- Syntax to create an index
CREATE INDEX index_name
ON table_name (column1, column2, ...);
      
-- Example: Creating an index on the "name" column of the "employees" table
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON employees (name);
✅ Example: Creating an Index for Faster Querying

-- Example table: employees
CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name VARCHAR(100),
    last_name VARCHAR(100),
    department VARCHAR(100)
);

-- Creating an index on "department" column to speed up querying by department
CREATE INDEX idx_department ON employees (department);
🔑 How Indexes Affect Query Performance
  • 🔍 When you query the "employees" table and filter by the "department" column, the index allows the database to quickly look up the rows with the desired department instead of scanning the entire table.
  • 🛑 Without the index, the database would need to perform a **full table scan**, which is slower on large tables.
✅ Removing an Index

To remove an index, use the DROP INDEX statement:


-- Syntax to drop an index
DROP INDEX index_name;

-- Example: Dropping the index created above
DROP INDEX idx_department;
📌 Types of Indexes in SQL
  • B-tree Index: The most common index type, based on a balanced tree structure, which allows for fast searching and sorting.
  • Unique Index: Ensures that all values in the indexed column(s) are unique. Automatically created for primary keys and unique constraints.
  • Full-text Index: Used for text-based searching on large text columns (e.g., searching for words in a document).
  • Bitmap Index: Best for columns with a low cardinality (e.g., gender, status), where there are only a few distinct values.
  • Hash Index: Uses a hash table for fast lookups, ideal for equality comparisons.
📌 Key Takeaways
  • 💡 Indexes speed up query performance, especially for read-heavy operations.
  • ⚡ Use indexes on columns that are frequently searched, filtered, or used in JOIN operations.
  • ⚠️ Over-indexing can harm write performance due to the additional cost of maintaining indexes.
  • 🔧 Remove unused or unnecessary indexes to save space and improve performance.

📌 What is a Race Condition?

A race condition occurs when two or more threads access shared data and try to modify it at the same time, leading to unpredictable or incorrect results.

In traditional HashMap, concurrent modifications by multiple threads can cause data inconsistency or infinite loops (in older Java versions).

✅ Role of ConcurrentHashMap

ConcurrentHashMap is part of java.util.concurrent package and is designed for high-concurrency scenarios.

It allows **multiple threads to read and write concurrently** without corrupting the internal state of the map.

🔒 Internal Mechanism to Avoid Race Conditions
  • 🧩 **Segmented Locking (before Java 8)**: The map was divided into multiple segments (like smaller maps), each with its own lock. Threads could lock only the segment they were accessing instead of the whole map.
  • ⚙️ **Synchronized Buckets & CAS (from Java 8)**:
    • Java 8 replaced segments with a **bucket array and linked lists / trees** inside buckets.
    • For write operations, it uses **synchronized blocks** on individual buckets (not whole map).
    • For atomic operations like putIfAbsent, it uses **Compare-And-Swap (CAS)** with the help of the `Unsafe` class.
  • ⚡ **No Global Lock**: Multiple threads can safely perform read/write operations on different buckets.
✅ Example: Safe Concurrent Access

import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

        // Thread 1
        new Thread(() -> {
            map.put("apple", 1);
        }).start();

        // Thread 2
        new Thread(() -> {
            map.putIfAbsent("apple", 2);
        }).start();
    }
}
❗ Why Not Use HashMap in Multithreaded Environment?
  • ❌ HashMap is not thread-safe.
  • ❌ May result in infinite loops due to corrupted structure under concurrent writes.
  • ❌ Requires external synchronization to make it thread-safe.
📌 Summary
  • 🔐 ConcurrentHashMap prevents race conditions using fine-grained locking and CAS techniques.
  • ⚙️ No need to manually synchronize access to the map.
  • 📈 Highly efficient for read-heavy concurrent applications.

📌 What is a Synchronized Map?

A synchronized map is a wrapper around a standard `HashMap` or `Map` that locks the **entire map** during every read or write operation using `Collections.synchronizedMap(map)` or manual synchronization.


Map<String, Integer> syncMap = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());
📌 What is ConcurrentHashMap?

ConcurrentHashMap is part of java.util.concurrent and allows concurrent read and write operations by using fine-grained locking or lock-free techniques.


ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> concurrentMap = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
📊 Comparison Table
Feature Synchronized Map ConcurrentHashMap
Locking Mechanism Whole map is locked for every operation Only part (bucket) is locked or CAS used
Read Operations Blocked if write is happening Can happen concurrently with writes
Performance Poor under high concurrency High performance under concurrency
Thread Safety Yes, but less efficient Yes, more efficient
Null Keys/Values Allows one null key and multiple null values Not allowed
Iteration Must be manually synchronized Weakly consistent and safe
Use Case Simple or small maps with low concurrency Large-scale multithreaded systems
✅ Advantages of ConcurrentHashMap
  • ⚡ Faster under concurrent operations
  • 🔒 Lock-free reads and fine-grained locking for writes
  • 🧵 Safe iteration in multithreaded environment
❌ Disadvantages of ConcurrentHashMap
  • 🚫 Does not allow null keys or values
  • ⚙️ Slightly complex internal structure
✅ Advantages of Synchronized Map
  • ✅ Simple to implement using existing HashMap
  • ✅ Allows null keys/values (same as regular HashMap)
❌ Disadvantages of Synchronized Map
  • 🐢 Poor performance under high concurrency
  • 🧱 Full map lock blocks all operations, even reads
  • 🧪 Needs external synchronization for iteration
📌 When to Use What?
  • 👉 Use ConcurrentHashMap for high-concurrency, performance-critical multithreaded applications (e.g., caches, shared state, etc.).
  • 👉 Use Synchronized Map for small-scale applications or where concurrency is limited.
📢 Summary

ConcurrentHashMap offers better concurrency and efficiency using fine-grained locking and is preferred in most multi-threaded environments, while synchronizedMap is simpler but slower due to global locking.

📌 The Problem: Multiple Bean Candidates

When Spring finds more than one bean of the same type for injection, it needs help to decide which one to use. That’s where @Primary and @Qualifier come in.

✅ @Primary — Global Default Bean

@Primary tells Spring to pick this bean by default when multiple beans of the same type exist.


@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    @Primary
    public Vehicle car() {
        return new Car();
    }

    @Bean
    public Vehicle bike() {
        return new Bike();
    }
}
      

@Autowired
private Vehicle vehicle; // Injects Car by default due to @Primary
  • ✅ Simple to use when there's one preferred bean
  • ⚠️ Only one @Primary allowed per type
🎯 @Qualifier — Explicit Bean Selection

@Qualifier is used when you want to specify *exactly* which bean to inject, even if another is marked @Primary.


@Autowired
@Qualifier("bike")
private Vehicle myBike; // Injects the 'bike' bean
  • ✅ Gives full control over which bean to inject
  • ✅ Can override @Primary choice
  • ⚠️ Must match the bean name or qualifier
❗ What If You Don't Use Either?

If multiple beans of the same type exist and neither @Primary nor @Qualifier is used, Spring will throw a:

NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
📌 Summary
  • @Primary: Use when one bean should be the default for that type
  • @Qualifier: Use when you want to select a specific bean explicitly
  • You can even combine both: Use @Primary as fallback and @Qualifier when needed

📌 What is Spring Boot Actuator?

Spring Boot Actuator provides **production-ready features** that help you monitor and manage your application — like checking health, metrics, logs, environment variables, and more.

✅ How to Enable Actuator

Step 1: Add the dependency in pom.xml


<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

Step 2: Enable endpoints in application.yml or application.properties


management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: "*"
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: always
🔍 Common Actuator Endpoints
  • /actuator/health – App health status
  • /actuator/info – App metadata
  • /actuator/beans – Loaded Spring beans
  • /actuator/metrics – JVM and custom metrics
  • /actuator/env – Environment properties
  • /actuator/mappings – Request mappings
  • /actuator/loggers – Logger levels
  • /actuator/threaddump – JVM thread info
🛠️ Creating a Custom Endpoint

Step 1: Create a class annotated with @Endpoint and @ReadOperation.


import org.springframework.boot.actuate.endpoint.annotation.Endpoint;
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.endpoint.annotation.ReadOperation;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
@Endpoint(id = "greet")
public class GreetEndpoint {

    @ReadOperation
    public String greet() {
        return "👋 Hello from custom actuator endpoint!";
    }
}

➡️ Access at: /actuator/greet

📦 Expose Only Specific Endpoints (Optional)

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,greet
🔐 Securing Actuator Endpoints
  • Actuator endpoints can expose sensitive info.
  • Secure using Spring Security or restrict access by IP/firewall in production.
📢 Summary
  • ✅ Actuator provides health checks, metrics, mappings, environment info, and more.
  • ⚙️ Custom endpoints are easy to create using @Endpoint and @ReadOperation.
  • 🔒 Use appropriate security configurations in production!

📌 Scenario Overview

In Java, when a subclass overrides a method from a superclass, there are rules regarding how it can handle or declare exceptions. These rules differ for:

  • ✔️ Checked Exceptions (Compile-time)
  • ✔️ Unchecked Exceptions (Runtime)
✅ Case 1: Superclass Method Throws RuntimeException (Unchecked)

class A {
    void m1() throws RuntimeException {
        System.out.println("A");
    }
}

class B extends A {
    @Override
    void m1() {
        System.out.println("B");
    }
}

Rules:

  • Subclass can ignore the exception — ✅ OK
  • Subclass can declare the same RuntimeException — ✅ OK
  • Subclass can declare a subclass of RuntimeException — ✅ OK
  • Subclass cannot declare a checked exception not thrown by parent — ❌ Compile error
⚠️ Case 2: Superclass Method Throws Checked Exception

class A {
    void m1() throws IOException {
        System.out.println("A");
    }
}

class B extends A {
    @Override
    void m1() throws FileNotFoundException {
        System.out.println("B");
    }
}

Rules:

  • Subclass must declare same or narrower checked exception — ✅ OK
  • Subclass cannot declare a broader exception — ❌ Compile error
  • Subclass can declare no exception at all — ✅ OK
❌ Case 3: Subclass Tries to Add New Checked Exception

class A {
    void m1() {
        System.out.println("A");
    }
}

class B extends A {
    @Override
    void m1() throws IOException {
        System.out.println("B");
    }
}

Result: ❌ Compile-Time Error

You can't add new checked exceptions in overridden methods if the superclass didn’t declare them.

🔄 Top to Bottom vs Bottom to Top
  • 🔽 Top → Bottom (Superclass to Subclass): Subclass must follow rules of the superclass method's exception contract
  • 🔼 Bottom → Top: Caller's handling depends on declared exceptions in the variable's type (polymorphism behavior)

A a = new B();  // Reference is of superclass A
a.m1();         // Must handle exceptions as per A's declaration
📢 Summary
  • ✔️ Runtime Exceptions can be ignored or reduced freely
  • ✔️ Checked Exceptions must follow the "same or narrower" rule
  • ❌ You can't introduce new checked exceptions in an overridden method
  • ✔️ Actual exception handling must match the **reference type**, not the **object type**

📌 What are Parallel Streams?

Parallel streams split the source data and process it in multiple threads, improving performance for large datasets. But they can introduce issues when shared mutable state is accessed.

⚠️ The Problem: Shared Mutable State

If you mutate a shared variable inside a parallel stream, it may result in race conditions and incorrect results.


List numbers = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
List result = new ArrayList<>();

numbers.parallelStream()
       .map(n -> n * 2)
       .forEach(result::add); // ❌ Not thread-safe

Problem: ArrayList is not thread-safe, so add() can cause data corruption.

✅ Solutions to Ensure Data Integrity
  • 🔒 Use thread-safe collections (e.g., Collections.synchronizedList, CopyOnWriteArrayList)
  • 🛠 Use stream's built-in collect() method (best practice)
  • 🏗 Avoid side effects in parallel streams
✔️ Recommended Approach — Use Collectors

List safeResult = numbers.parallelStream()
                                  .map(n -> n * 2)
                                  .collect(Collectors.toList());

This uses an internal thread-safe collector and avoids side-effects.

✔️ Thread-Safe List (Alternative)

List safeList = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());

numbers.parallelStream()
       .map(n -> n * 2)
       .forEach(safeList::add);  // ✅ Now thread-safe

⚠️ Still not as clean or efficient as using collect()

📢 Summary
  • ❌ Don’t use shared mutable state inside parallel streams
  • ✅ Prefer collect() to aggregate results
  • ✅ Use thread-safe structures when mutation is necessary
  • 🔁 Always test parallel code under concurrency to ensure correctness

📌 What is ClassNotFoundException?
  • ✅ It's a checked exception (must be caught or declared)
  • 💥 Thrown when a class is not found at runtime using methods like Class.forName(), ClassLoader.loadClass()
  • 🧠 It happens when you try to load a class by name and it's not in the classpath

try {
    Class.forName("com.example.MyClass");
} catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
    e.printStackTrace();  // Class file not found in classpath
}
📌 What is NoClassDefFoundError?
  • ❌ It's an unchecked error (subclass of Error)
  • ⚠️ Thrown when a class was present during compile time but is missing at runtime
  • 🧠 Often caused when a required class is removed or not deployed correctly

MyClass obj = new MyClass(); // If MyClass.class is missing at runtime => NoClassDefFoundError
✅ Key Differences
Feature ClassNotFoundException NoClassDefFoundError
Type Checked Exception Error
When Thrown? Class is not found when loaded dynamically Class was available during compile-time but missing at runtime
Cause Misconfigured classpath or missing JAR at runtime Corrupt or missing class file at runtime
Fix Ensure class is available in classpath for dynamic loading Ensure all compile-time dependencies are packaged and deployed
🧪 Example Comparison

// ClassNotFoundException (via reflection)
try {
    Class.forName("com.abc.NonExistingClass");
} catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
    System.out.println("Caught ClassNotFoundException");
}

// NoClassDefFoundError (direct instantiation)
NonExistingClass obj = new NonExistingClass();  // Throws NoClassDefFoundError if class was removed
🔍 How to Prevent Them?
  • ✅ Keep your build artifacts clean (Maven/Gradle)
  • ✅ Use ClassLoader.getResource() or dependency analyzers to validate classpath
  • ✅ Use tools like JAR scanners and runtime classpath verifiers
📢 Summary
  • 📦 ClassNotFoundException → Happens during dynamic loading using reflection
  • 📦 NoClassDefFoundError → Happens when class exists at compile-time but missing during runtime
  • 🎯 Both are related to classpath issues, but at different stages

📌 What is Exception Hierarchy in Java?
  • Throwable (top-level)
  • ├── Error (JVM/internal issues)
  • └── Exception
  •     ├── Checked Exceptions (e.g., IOException)
  •     └── Unchecked Exceptions = RuntimeException and its subclasses
⚠️ Difference Between Exception and RuntimeException
Feature Checked Exception (Exception) Unchecked Exception (RuntimeException)
Handling Must be declared or caught Optional to handle
Compiler Enforcement Yes No
Common Usage External failures (I/O, SQL, network) Programming errors (null, invalid args)
Spring Boot Preference Rarely used Preferred for business exceptions
✅ Why Spring Boot Uses RuntimeException for Custom Exceptions?
  • 💡 Spring encourages use of unchecked exceptions to avoid boilerplate try-catch everywhere.
  • 🚀 Helps you write cleaner business logic (throw custom exceptions without declaring in method signature)
  • 🎯 Integrates smoothly with @ControllerAdvice for global exception handling
  • 📦 Most of Spring’s own exceptions (like HttpClientErrorException) are RuntimeExceptions
🛠 Example

// ✅ Recommended: Extending RuntimeException
public class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public ResourceNotFoundException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}

// ❌ Verbose: Extending Exception
public class ResourceCheckedException extends Exception {
    public ResourceCheckedException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}
      

@RestController
public class UserController {
    @GetMapping("/user/{id}")
    public User getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        throw new ResourceNotFoundException("User not found!");
    }
}
      

@ControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<String> handleNotFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(ex.getMessage());
    }
}
📢 Summary
  • ✅ Spring Boot prefers RuntimeException for custom exceptions for cleaner, simpler code
  • 📜 Checked exceptions are still valid, but make code more verbose and harder to manage in large apps
  • 🧠 Use @ControllerAdvice to handle all exceptions in one place for clean separation of concerns

📌 Scenario Description

You're overriding a method from a parent class, but in the subclass you're throwing a broader exception. Let's see the exact example:


class A {
    public void m1() throws ArithmeticException {
        // Unchecked exception
    }
}

class B extends A {
    @Override
    public void m1() throws Exception { // ❌ Compile-time Error
        // Trying to throw a checked broader exception
    }
}
🚫 Why Does This Fail?
  • Java does **not allow overriding methods to declare broader (more general) checked exceptions** than the superclass method.
  • ArithmeticException is an unchecked exception (subclass of RuntimeException), while Exception is a checked exception.
  • This breaks the **method contract** of the superclass, which says: “I won’t throw a checked exception”.
✅ Valid Overriding Rules for Exceptions
  • You can throw the same exception as the superclass.
  • You can throw a subclass of the exception declared in the superclass.
  • You can remove the exception completely in the subclass.
  • You cannot add new or broader checked exceptions.
💡 Valid Example

class A {
    public void m1() throws IOException {
        // Checked exception
    }
}

class B extends A {
    @Override
    public void m1() throws FileNotFoundException { // ✅ Subclass of IOException
        // Valid override
    }
}
📢 Summary
  • ✅ In overriding, you can throw unchecked exceptions freely.
  • ❌ You cannot throw broader or new checked exceptions in the overridden method.
  • 🧠 Java does this to ensure subclass methods do not violate the expectations set by the superclass.

📌 What is Relational Mapping?

Relational mapping is the process of mapping Java classes (entities) to database tables using ORM (Object Relational Mapping) tools like JPA and Hibernate.

It helps in automatically managing CRUD operations and relationships like One-to-One, One-to-Many, etc., by just using annotations in your entity classes.

✅ Technologies Involved
  • Spring Boot: Provides abstraction and configuration ease
  • JPA (Java Persistence API): A specification for ORM in Java
  • Hibernate: A popular implementation of JPA
🧱 Entity Class Example

@Entity
@Table(name = "users")
public class User {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(name = "username", nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String username;

    @OneToOne(mappedBy = "user", cascade = CascadeType.ALL)
    private Profile profile;
}
🔄 Types of Mappings with Examples
1️⃣ One-To-One Mapping

@Entity
public class Profile {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;

    private String bio;

    @OneToOne
    @JoinColumn(name = "user_id")  // Foreign Key
    private User user;
}
  • @OneToOne: Specifies one-to-one relationship
  • @JoinColumn: Foreign key column name in table
  • cascade: Cascade operation (e.g., ALL, PERSIST)
  • mappedBy: Tells Hibernate this is the inverse side
2️⃣ One-To-Many / Many-To-One

@Entity
public class Department {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "department")
    private List<Employee> employees;
}

@Entity
public class Employee {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @ManyToOne
    @JoinColumn(name = "dept_id")
    private Department department;
}
  • @OneToMany: One entity has many children
  • @ManyToOne: Each child refers to one parent
  • mappedBy: Defines owner/inverse side
3️⃣ Many-To-Many

@Entity
public class Student {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @ManyToMany
    @JoinTable(
      name = "student_course",
      joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"),
      inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id"))
    private List<Course> courses;
}

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;

    private String title;
}
  • @ManyToMany: Represents many-to-many association
  • @JoinTable: Defines join table and keys
  • @JoinColumn: Column definition inside join table
⚙️ Common Annotation Properties
  • cascade: Propagate operations like save, delete
  • fetch: LAZY or EAGER loading
  • mappedBy: Defines ownership (inverse side)
  • orphanRemoval: Removes children when removed from parent list
  • optional: Whether the relationship can be null
📢 Summary
  • 🔗 Relational Mapping connects Java objects to DB tables
  • 🧰 JPA annotations like @OneToOne, @ManyToOne simplify the work
  • 🧠 Understanding annotations & properties helps manage relationships and performance efficiently

📌 What is Dirty Checking?

Dirty Checking is a feature in Hibernate (and JPA providers) that automatically detects changes made to a persistent object and synchronizes those changes to the database during a transaction commit — without explicitly calling an update method.

It ensures the database is kept in sync with the state of objects in memory.

✅ Example of Dirty Checking

@Transactional
public void updateUser(Long id) {
    User user = entityManager.find(User.class, id); // object loaded in persistence context
    user.setUsername("newName"); // state modified
    // No call to entityManager.merge() or save()
    // Hibernate tracks the change automatically
}

When the transaction commits, Hibernate checks what fields were modified and generates the appropriate SQL UPDATE query.

⚙️ How Does It Work Internally?
  • Hibernate keeps a snapshot of the object's original state when it is loaded.
  • During transaction flush (before commit), it compares current object state to the original snapshot.
  • If any field changed ⇒ Hibernate fires an UPDATE query.
📌 When Does Dirty Checking Happen?
  • During transaction commit
  • During flush() (explicitly or automatically)
✅ Benefits of Dirty Checking
  • 🔄 No need to explicitly call update or merge
  • 📉 Reduces boilerplate code
  • 🧠 Simplifies object management in transactions
⚠️ Pitfalls
  • ❗ May lead to unintended updates if not careful
  • ❗ Extra updates if flushing too frequently
  • ❗ Requires proper transaction boundaries
📢 Summary

Dirty Checking is an automatic mechanism in Hibernate that detects changes in managed entities and syncs them with the database at commit. It’s powerful and reduces the need for manual updates, but should be used with care to avoid unnecessary SQL updates.

📌 What is PUT?
  • PUT is used to update or replace the entire resource.
  • If the resource exists, it will be completely replaced with the request payload.
  • If it doesn’t exist, PUT may create a new resource (idempotent).

// Original resource:
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Alice",
  "email": "alice@example.com"
}

// PUT Request:
PUT /users/1
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Alice Updated",
  "email": "alice.new@example.com"
}
📌 What is PATCH?
  • PATCH is used to partially update a resource.
  • Only the specified fields are updated; others remain unchanged.
  • PATCH is ideal for performance and bandwidth efficiency.

// PATCH Request:
PATCH /users/1
{
  "email": "alice.updated@example.com"
}

// Only the "email" field is updated
🔍 Key Differences
Feature PUT PATCH
Update Type Full Resource Update Partial Resource Update
Payload Complete object Only updated fields
Idempotency Yes Yes (ideally)
Overwrites Data Yes No
Use Case Replace object entirely Update a few fields
📦 When to Use PUT?
  • When updating the whole resource
  • When you're replacing an entity
  • When working with clients that send full data sets
✂️ When to Use PATCH?
  • When modifying only a part of the resource
  • When minimizing data sent over network
  • When you want lightweight and fast updates
📢 Summary
  • PUT = Replace entire resource (send full object)
  • PATCH = Modify partial data (send only changes)
  • Both are useful depending on context — choose wisely based on performance and update requirements.

📌 What is Idempotency?

Idempotent means that an operation can be repeated multiple times and the result will always be the same.

For an HTTP method, it means that performing the same request multiple times has no additional effect after the first one.

✅ Why is PUT Idempotent?
  • PUT is used to replace a resource entirely with the data sent in the request body.
  • If you send the same request multiple times, the resource will remain unchanged after the first update.
  • For example, whether you call PUT once or many times with the same data, the resource remains the same.

PUT /user/1
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "John",
  "email": "john@example.com"
}
🔄 Example of Idempotency
  • First Request (PUT): 
    
PUT /user/1
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "John",
  "email": "john@example.com"
}
  • Second Request (PUT with the same data): 
    
PUT /user/1
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "John",
  "email": "john@example.com"
}
  • In both cases, the result is the same — the resource for user with ID 1 is updated with the same data.
📌 Common Mistake with PUT Idempotency
  • PUT is idempotent **only if the server respects idempotency** (i.e., no side effects like adding a timestamp or random values on each request).
  • For example, if the server adds a timestamp to every PUT request, then it would no longer be idempotent because the state would change with each call.
⚠️ Conclusion: Is PUT Idempotent?
  • Yes, PUT is idempotent as long as the same data is sent in every request.
  • Subsequent PUT requests with the same data will result in the same resource state without any side effects.
  • If the server behaves correctly, PUT will always result in the same state regardless of how many times it's called.

📌 What is Swagger?

Swagger is a toolset used to design, build, document, and consume REST APIs. It generates interactive API documentation that can be accessed via a UI.

Swagger allows you to generate API documentation directly from your codebase, ensuring that the documentation is always in sync with your API implementation.

✅ Benefits of Using Swagger
  • 📖 Automatically generated API documentation
  • 💻 Easy-to-use interactive interface for testing APIs
  • 🔄 Always up-to-date with the code
  • 🛠 Supports multiple languages and frameworks
⚙️ How to Integrate Swagger in Spring Boot?

Follow these steps to integrate Swagger into your Spring Boot application:

Step 1: Add Swagger Dependencies



  io.springfox
  springfox-boot-starter
  3.0.0
Step 2: Configure Swagger

import springfox.documentation.swagger2.annotations.EnableSwagger2;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import springfox.documentation.builders.PathSelectors;
import springfox.documentation.builders.RequestHandlerSelectors;
import springfox.documentation.spi.DocumentationType;
import springfox.documentation.spring.web.plugins.Docket;

@Configuration
@EnableSwagger2
public class SwaggerConfig {
    @Bean
    public Docket api() {
        return new Docket(DocumentationType.SWAGGER_2)
                .select()
                .apis(RequestHandlerSelectors.basePackage("com.example.controller"))
                .paths(PathSelectors.any())
                .build();
    }
}
Step 3: Access Swagger UI

Once the application is running, you can access the Swagger UI at:

http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui/
✅ How to Document API Endpoints?
  • Use @Api to describe the controller class.
  • Use @ApiOperation to describe individual methods.
  • Use @ApiParam for detailed parameter descriptions.
Example of Documentation

import io.swagger.annotations.Api;
import io.swagger.annotations.ApiOperation;
import io.swagger.annotations.ApiParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@Api(tags = "User API")
@RestController
public class UserController {

    @ApiOperation(value = "Get User by ID", notes = "Fetches a user by their ID")
    @GetMapping("/user")
    public String getUserById(
        @ApiParam(value = "ID of the user", required = true) @RequestParam Long id) {
        return "User ID: " + id;
    }
}
⚙️ Available Swagger Configurations
  • Docket Bean: The central configuration for Swagger, which includes API documentation settings like endpoints and packages to scan.
  • API Selector: Use RequestHandlerSelectors and PathSelectors to filter which controllers and methods are exposed.
  • Custom API Info: You can customize the title, description, terms of service, version, etc., in the documentation.
    • 
public Docket api() {
    return new Docket(DocumentationType.SWAGGER_2)
            .select()
            .apis(RequestHandlerSelectors.basePackage("com.example"))
            .paths(PathSelectors.any())
            .build()
            .apiInfo(new ApiInfo(
                    "My API", 
                    "API Documentation", 
                    "1.0", 
                    "Terms of Service", 
                    new Contact("John Doe", "www.johndoe.com", "john.doe@example.com"),
                    "License", 
                    "License URL", 
                    Collections.emptyList()));
}
📌 Summary
  • Swagger simplifies API documentation and testing.
  • It integrates seamlessly with Spring Boot to generate interactive API docs.
  • You can configure Swagger using Docket and filter what to expose using various selectors.

📌 What is Spring Security?

Spring Security is a powerful and customizable authentication and access control framework for Java applications, especially for Spring-based applications. It provides protection against many security threats such as CSRF, session fixation, etc.

✅ Components of Spring Security
  • Authentication Manager: Handles authentication requests and determines whether the credentials are valid.
  • Authentication Provider: Validates the credentials of a user, typically used with a service like a database or LDAP.
  • Security Filters: Intercepts incoming requests to provide security services like authentication and authorization checks.
  • Access Decision Manager: Makes decisions about whether a user can access a particular resource based on their roles or permissions.
  • Security Context: Stores details of the current authenticated user throughout a session.
  • Authorization: Determines whether the authenticated user has the necessary permissions to access resources.
  • CSRF Protection: Protects the application from Cross-Site Request Forgery attacks.
  • Session Management: Manages user sessions, including security-related actions like session fixation protection.
⚙️ Example of Spring Security in Spring Boot 3
Step 1: Add Dependencies



  org.springframework.boot
  spring-boot-starter-security
Step 2: Configure Spring Security

Define a custom configuration class for security settings:


import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.EnableWebSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter;

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter {

    @Override
    protected void configure(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeRequests()
            .antMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .antMatchers("/user/**").hasAnyRole("USER", "ADMIN")
            .antMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
            .and()
            .formLogin()
            .permitAll()
            .and()
            .logout()
            .permitAll();
    }
}
Step 3: User Details Service

Create a service to load user-specific data:


import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetails;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UsernameNotFoundException;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class CustomUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {

    @Override
    public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) throws UsernameNotFoundException {
        // Example of a hardcoded user (you would typically fetch this from a database)
        if ("admin".equals(username)) {
            return User.withUsername("admin")
                    .password("{noop}admin123")  // {noop} is used to indicate no encryption for simplicity
                    .roles("ADMIN")
                    .build();
        } else if ("user".equals(username)) {
            return User.withUsername("user")
                    .password("{noop}user123")
                    .roles("USER")
                    .build();
        }
        throw new UsernameNotFoundException("User not found");
    }
}
Step 4: Access Control

Control access to different parts of your application based on roles:
